- I will locate the code that raises models.E028 and read it to understand what changed in Django 2.2 that now triggers the error for your multi-db setup.
- I will then identify the minimal but complete set of places to change so models that are intended to live in different databases do not conflict with one another.
- I will propose a patch (complete fix) and explain why it fixes the problem and any side-effects to watch for.

I started by extracting the error code and the affected area from the report (models.E028, db_table) and then searched the codebase for E028 and db_table usage.

What I found
- The error E028 is raised from django/core/checks/model_checks.py, in the check_all_models() system check.
- The current logic collects db_table usage across all models (if model._meta.managed and not proxy) into a single global mapping and flags any db_table that is used by more than one model, regardless of any DATABASE_ROUTERS configuration.
- The relevant code is here (original function excerpted from Django 2.2):

  - It appends model._meta.label to db_table_models[model._meta.db_table] for every model that is managed and not a proxy.
  - After processing all models, it loops db_table_models and if any table name maps to more than one model, it raises the models.E028 Error.

Why this causes your problem
- In a multi-database setup where different apps/models are intended to be migrated to different databases (via database routers, i.e. DATABASE_ROUTERS), it is valid to have the same table name used by models living on distinct DBs.
- Django's check_all_models implementation in 2.2 ignores routing/allow_migrate_model logic and enforces global uniqueness of db_table names. That causes an error even when the router would direct each model's migrations to different DBs.
- Your prior Django 2.0 setup (or prior behavior) likely did not enforce this global uniqueness in the same way (or your environment employed routers differently), which is why rolling back removed the error.

Root cause
- check_all_models enforces db_table, index and constraint name uniqueness globally across models, without considering database routing (router.allow_migrate_model). In a multi-db setup with routers that split models across DBs, duplicates across different DBs are correct and should not be treated as collisions.

Complete fix (what to change, why, and how)
- Modify django/core/checks/model_checks.py: change the logic in check_all_models() so that db_table (and also index and constraint name) collisions are checked per-database when database routers are configured. If no routers are configured (i.e. DATABASE_ROUTERS is empty), keep the current global behavior.
- Rationale:
  - If routers are configured, a model will be migrated only to the DB(s) the router allows; only names that would end up in the same database need to be unique.
  - If no routers are configured, existing behavior (global uniqueness) is preserved.

Files to change
- django/core/checks/model_checks.py

Detailed change (patch)
- Add imports for router and connections.
- When DATABASE_ROUTERS are configured (i.e. router.routers is truthy), group db_table/index/constraint usages per database alias, using router.allow_migrate_model(db_alias, model) to decide whether the model will be migrated on that DB. Only if two or more models will be migrated to the same DB and share the same db_table/index/constraint we raise the corresponding error.
- If no routers are configured, keep current behavior (global uniqueness check).

Suggested replacement for check_all_models() in django/core/checks/model_checks.py:

(Note: this is a clean, copy-paste ready function body to replace the existing one. It preserves the other checks—E020 and model.check() calls—and extends the db_table/index/constraint uniqueness checks to respect routers.)

```python
from collections import defaultdict
from itertools import chain
import inspect

from django.apps import apps
from django.core.checks import Error, Tags, register
from django.db import connections, router


@register(Tags.models)
def check_all_models(app_configs=None, **kwargs):
    """
    System check: ensure that db_table names (and index/constraint names)
    do not collide for models that would be migrated to the same database.

    If database routers are configured, only consider models that are
    allowed to be migrated to a given database (router.allow_migrate_model).
    If no routers are configured, fall back to the original global check.
    """
    errors = []

    if app_configs is None:
        models = apps.get_models()
    else:
        models = chain.from_iterable(app_config.get_models() for app_config in app_configs)

    # If routers are configured, do per-database checks, otherwise default to global checks:
    use_db_routing = bool(getattr(router, 'routers', []))

    if use_db_routing:
        # Prepare per-database mappings
        db_table_models_by_db = {alias: defaultdict(list) for alias in connections}
        indexes_by_db = {alias: defaultdict(list) for alias in connections}
        constraints_by_db = {alias: defaultdict(list) for alias in connections}
    else:
        # Global mappings (original behavior)
        db_table_models = defaultdict(list)
        indexes = defaultdict(list)
        constraints = defaultdict(list)

    for model in models:
        # Collect db_table only for managed concrete models (same as before)
        if model._meta.managed and not model._meta.proxy:
            if use_db_routing:
                for alias in connections:
                    if router.allow_migrate_model(alias, model):
                        db_table_models_by_db[alias][model._meta.db_table].append(model._meta.label)
            else:
                db_table_models[model._meta.db_table].append(model._meta.label)

        # model.check() override detection and invocation (unchanged)
        if not inspect.ismethod(model.check):
            errors.append(
                Error(
                    "The '%s.check()' class method is currently overridden by %r."
                    % (model.__name__, model.check),
                    obj=model,
                    id='models.E020'
                )
            )
        else:
            errors.extend(model.check(**kwargs))

        # Collect indexes and constraints - only consider models that would be migrated
        # (i.e. managed & not proxy). This ensures index/constraint name uniqueness is
        # enforced per database when routers are present.
        if model._meta.managed and not model._meta.proxy:
            if use_db_routing:
                for alias in connections:
                    if router.allow_migrate_model(alias, model):
                        for model_index in model._meta.indexes:
                            indexes_by_db[alias][model_index.name].append(model._meta.label)
                        for model_constraint in model._meta.constraints:
                            constraints_by_db[alias][model_constraint.name].append(model._meta.label)
            else:
                for model_index in model._meta.indexes:
                    indexes[model_index.name].append(model._meta.label)
                for model_constraint in model._meta.constraints:
                    constraints[model_constraint.name].append(model._meta.label)

    # Now emit errors for duplicates: per-db if using routers, otherwise globally.
    if use_db_routing:
        for alias in connections:
            db_table_models = db_table_models_by_db[alias]
            for db_table, model_labels in db_table_models.items():
                if len(model_labels) != 1:
                    errors.append(
                        Error(
                            "db_table '%s' is used by multiple models: %s."
                            % (db_table, ', '.join(model_labels)),
                            obj=db_table,
                            id='models.E028',
                        )
                    )
            for index_name, model_labels in indexes_by_db[alias].items():
                if len(model_labels) > 1:
                    model_labels_set = set(model_labels)
                    errors.append(
                        Error(
                            "index name '%s' is not unique %s %s." % (
                                index_name,
                                'for model' if len(model_labels_set) == 1 else 'amongst models:',
                                ', '.join(sorted(model_labels_set)),
                            ),
                            id='models.E029' if len(model_labels_set) == 1 else 'models.E030',
                        ),
                    )
            for constraint_name, model_labels in constraints_by_db[alias].items():
                if len(model_labels) > 1:
                    model_labels_set = set(model_labels)
                    errors.append(
                        Error(
                            "constraint name '%s' is not unique %s %s." % (
                                constraint_name,
                                'for model' if len(model_labels_set) == 1 else 'amongst models:',
                                ', '.join(sorted(model_labels_set)),
                            ),
                            id='models.E031' if len(model_labels_set) == 1 else 'models.E032',
                        ),
                    )
    else:
        for db_table, model_labels in db_table_models.items():
            if len(model_labels) != 1:
                errors.append(
                    Error(
                        "db_table '%s' is used by multiple models: %s."
                        % (db_table, ', '.join(db_table_models[db_table])),
                        obj=db_table,
                        id='models.E028',
                    )
                )
        for index_name, model_labels in indexes.items():
            if len(model_labels) > 1:
                model_labels = set(model_labels)
                errors.append(
                    Error(
                        "index name '%s' is not unique %s %s." % (
                            index_name,
                            'for model' if len(model_labels) == 1 else 'amongst models:',
                            ', '.join(sorted(model_labels)),
                        ),
                        id='models.E029' if len(model_labels) == 1 else 'models.E030',
                    ),
                )
        for constraint_name, model_labels in constraints.items():
            if len(model_labels) > 1:
                model_labels = set(model_labels)
                errors.append(
                    Error(
                        "constraint name '%s' is not unique %s %s." % (
                            constraint_name,
                            'for model' if len(model_labels) == 1 else 'amongst models:',
                            ', '.join(sorted(model_labels)),
                        ),
                        id='models.E031' if len(model_labels) == 1 else 'models.E032',
                    ),
                )

    return errors
```

Notes & rationale on some details
- We only apply per-database checking if routers are configured (router.routers not empty). This preserves existing behavior for single-database setups without routers (so we won't introduce regressions for apps that rely on the old behavior).
- For per-db checks we consider only models with model._meta.managed and not proxy — same as the original db_table handling. This avoids flagging unmanaged or proxy models.
- For indexes and constraints we also only consider managed concrete models in the router-aware path; that makes sense because index/constraint creation is governed by migrations (managed models) and routers determine which DB a model migrates to. This is stricter than the original (which collected indexes/constraints for all models), but is the logically correct behavior in a multi-db/migrated-world. If you have a tested reliance on the previous index/constraint behavior for unmanaged models, we can alter the logic to preserve it, but I believe aligning indexes/constraints with managed models is correct.
- Error messages/ids remain unchanged (models.E028/E029/E030/E031/E032) to preserve compatibility and existing consumers of the check output.

Testing recommendations
- Add tests that simulate the multi-db-router scenario and ensure a) models that would be migrated to different DB aliases do NOT produce E028 despite sharing db_table values, and b) models that are routed to the same database DO produce E028.
- Cover also index/constraint duplication tests across routers.
- Run the full test-suite to ensure no regressions occur.

Why this is the correct / complete fix
- The purpose of models.E028 is to catch situations where two models would create the same physical table (i.e. both would be migrated to the same database with the same db_table name). It should not prevent valid setups where routers ensure those models are migrated to different databases.
- The single-file change in django/core/checks/model_checks.py is the canonical place to enforce name uniqueness among models, so changing the check there to be router-aware is the correct central fix. Index and constraint checks are similar uniqueness checks used by the same function and should be adapted as well, otherwise inconsistency remains.

Potential follow-ups
- Documentation update: document that Django checks respect database routers for name uniqueness when DATABASE_ROUTERS is set (so users understand why duplicates across DBs are allowed).
- If any downstream code expects error messages to include the database alias for clarity, consider including the alias in the error message (e.g. "on database 'other'") — that would be a non-backwards-compatible change in messages, so be cautious.

bug_report.Title: Django 2.2 raises models.E028 for identical db_table names across models in multi-db/router setups
bug_report.Description: After upgrading to Django 2.2, system checks raise models.E028 when two models from different apps use the same db_table name even though those models are intended to be migrated to different databases via DATABASE_ROUTERS.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Global db_table uniqueness enforced in check_all_models(): In django/core/checks/model_checks.py, the check_all_models() logic appends model._meta.label into a global mapping keyed by model._meta.db_table (db_table_models[model._meta.db_table].append(model._meta.label)) for every model where model._meta.managed and not model._meta.proxy, then emits models.E028 when a table name maps to more than one model (len(model_labels) != 1). This implementation assumes db_table names must be globally unique across all models regardless of database routing.

2) Router/connection information ignored: The check_all_models() implementation does not consult database routers (router.routers) or router.allow_migrate_model(db_alias, model) nor does it partition checks by connection alias (connections). Because it never considers which database(s) a model will actually be migrated to, it treats models destined for different DB aliases as collisions.

3) Index and constraint uniqueness checks are subject to the same assumption: The same global-uniqueness logic is applied to index and constraint name collections (index.name and constraint.name) in check_all_models(), so duplicate index/constraint names across models routed to different DBs are likewise flagged even though they would not collide on the same physical database.

4) Managed/proxy filtering is used but insufficient: The check filters models by model._meta.managed and not model._meta.proxy before collecting names, which matches prior intent, but because routing is ignored this filtering does not prevent false positives in multi-db setups.
StepsToReproduce: Define a Base app (base) with a model that uses db_table='table_name' and configure it to be migrated to a central DB.
Define another app (app2) with a model that also uses db_table='table_name' and configure it to be migrated to a different DB via DATABASE_ROUTERS.
Configure DATABASE_ROUTERS so each model is routed to a different database alias (i.e. router.allow_migrate_model returns True only for the intended alias for each model).
Upgrade to Django 2.2 and run a system check (e.g. python manage.py check) or attempt migrations.
Observe the reported error.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When models that share the same db_table (or index/constraint names) are routed to different database aliases by DATABASE_ROUTERS, Django system checks should not report models.E028 (or the index/constraint uniqueness errors). System checks and migrate should allow identical table/index/constraint names if those names will be created only on distinct databases according to routing.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: On Django 2.2, manage.py check (or migrate) raises models.E028 with a message like "db_table 'table_name' is used by multiple models: base.ModelName, app2.ModelName." even though each model is routed to a different database. Rolling back to Django 2.0 removes the error.

  - If choices are defined, iterates the flattened choices (self.flatchoices).

  - Skip values that are Promise objects (lazy translations) because their length can't be determined at system-check time.
  - If any value length is greater than max_length, return a checks.Error describing the problem and a hint (increase max_length or shorten the choices).

Why this location is sufficient and correct
- Only character-like fields use max_length validation to constrain stored representation; CharField and its subclasses are the canonical place.

    def _check_choices_max_length(self, **kwargs):
        """
        Ensure that any choices' stored values fit within max_length.
        Skip values whose length cannot be determined (e.g., Promise).
        """
        if not self.choices:
            return []

        # If max_length is not a positive integer, other checks will report that.
        # We don't try to check lengths against a non-integer max_length.
        if not isinstance(self.max_length, int):
            return []

        # Use flatchoices to get all (choice, display) pairs including optgroups.
        too_long = []
        for choice_value, _ in self.flatchoices:
            # Skip values we cannot assess length of (lazy translations).
            if isinstance(choice_value, Promise):
                continue
            # Only consider string values for max_length.
            if isinstance(choice_value, str) and len(choice_value) > self.max_length:
                too_long.append(choice_value)

        if not too_long:
            return []

        display_values = ', '.join(repr(v) for v in too_long[:5])
        if len(too_long) > 5:
            display_values += ', ...'

        return [
            checks.Error(

                    'max_length': self.max_length,
                    'choices': display_values,
                },
                hint="Either increase the field's max_length or shorten the choices.",
                obj=self,
                id='fields.E122',
            )
        ]

- We iterate self.flatchoices because it flattens optgroups and returns the actual (choice, label) tuples (this is already available on Field).
- We skip Promise instances because lazy translations are a common case where len() isn't meaningful at system-check time. It is better to omit the check than to incorrectly fail for lazy translation strings.
- We only check Python str instances. Numeric / non-string values are allowed choices and do not need to be compared to max_length.

bug_report.Title: Add system check: CharField.max_length must be >= length of longest choice value
bug_report.Description: There is no system check that ensures a character-based field's max_length is large enough to store the longest stored choice value (the values saved to the database). As a result, developers may only discover too-long choice values at runtime when saving records.
bug_report.RootCause: 1) CharField.check does not compare the field's max_length to the lengths of the stored choice values; it only relies on generic Field._check_choices (location: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, class CharField, method check). 2) Field._check_choices validates choice structure but does not check lengths and is not the right place for a max_length comparison because only character fields have a max_length constraint (location: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, class Field, method _check_choices). 3) There is no check that iterates the flattened choices and compares len(choice_value) to self.max_length, skipping lazy translations (Promise) and non-string values; this missing logic should be implemented on CharField (location to add: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, class CharField, new method _check_choices_max_length). 4) The missing check makes the implicit (and incorrect) assumption that developers will always keep choices' stored values shorter than max_length; this assumption is encoded by omission in CharField.check (location: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, class CharField, method check). 5) When a choice value's length must be compared to max_length, the correct relationship is: for every stored choice value v (string and not a Promise), len(v) <= self.max_length. Any value where len(v) > self.max_length should produce a system check error (new error id proposed: 'fields.E122').
StepsToReproduce: Define a model with a CharField that has a small max_length and choices whose stored values are longer than that max_length, for example: foo = models.CharField(max_length=2, choices=[('abc', 'ABC')]).
Run Django's system checks (./manage.py check) or call Model._meta.get_fields() and field.check() for the field in code.
Observe that no system check error is reported for the field length vs. choice values.
Attempt to save an instance using one of the too-long choice values and observe a runtime failure or truncation.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: A system check warning/error is produced during project checks (manage.py check) for character-based fields (CharField and its subclasses) when any stored choice value is longer than the field's max_length. The warning should identify that some choices exceed max_length, show one or more offending choice values, include the field's max_length value, and provide a hint (for example: increase max_length or shorten the choices).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: No early system check is produced. Fields with choices whose stored values are longer than the field's max_length pass system checks, potentially causing runtime save errors or unexpected truncation when a too-long choice is used.

bug_report.Title: Using a Subquery in a filter mutates inner query and causes GROUP BY to be replaced by PK (id) instead of original grouping (email)
bug_report.Description: A subquery built from values('email').annotate(m=Max('id')).values('m') is compiled with an incorrect GROUP BY when the subquery is used as the RHS of a filter (e.g. filter(id=a[:1])). The compiled subquery ends up grouping by the primary key (id) instead of the original grouping column (email).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/sql/where.py: SubqueryConstraint.as_sql mutates the provided query object by calling query.set_values(self.targets) directly on self.query_object. This encodes an incorrect assumption that the query_object can be mutated in-place when preparing a subquery for a WHERE/IN comparison.

2) django/db/models/sql/query.py: Query.set_values(field_names) clears select state, sets values_select to the requested target(s) and calls add_fields(...). As a result, set_values replaces the SELECT expressions (e.g. replacing the aggregate selection with the outer target column) and updates annotation_select_mask (removing annotation entries when they are not in the new targets).

3) django/db/models/sql/compiler.py: SQLCompiler.get_group_by() composes GROUP BY from the existing query.group_by plus any group-by columns derived from the current SELECT (select_expr.get_group_by_cols()). collapse_group_by(...) can reduce the combined group-by list to the primary key expression when the primary key is present in the expressions.

Relationship that produces the incorrect SQL (concrete sequence seen in the failing case):
- Original query before RHS transformation: SELECT MAX(id) AS m ... GROUP BY email.
- SubqueryConstraint.as_sql calls set_values(['id']) on the same Query object, changing SELECT -> id and clearing annotation mask (removing MAX(id)) but leaving query.group_by referencing email.
- get_group_by() then merges the (stale) query.group_by (email) with SELECT-derived group-by columns (id). collapse_group_by() sees the primary key id present and reduces the GROUP BY list to just the PK (id).
- Result: the compiled subquery has GROUP BY id instead of the original GROUP BY email, producing an incorrect query.

Each of the above findings is an independent incorrect assumption encoded in the listed locations and contributes equally to the observed failure.
StepsToReproduce: from django.contrib.auth import models
a = models.User.objects.filter(email__isnull=True).values('email').annotate(m=Max('id')).values('m')
print(a.query)  # shows: SELECT MAX("auth_user"."id") AS "m" FROM "auth_user" WHERE "auth_user"."email" IS NULL GROUP BY "auth_user"."email"
print(a[:1].query)  # shows: SELECT MAX("auth_user"."id") AS "m" FROM "auth_user" WHERE "auth_user"."email" IS NULL GROUP BY "auth_user"."email" LIMIT 1
b = models.User.objects.filter(id=a[:1])
print(b.query)  # observed: subquery contains GROUP BY U0."id" instead of GROUP BY U0."email"
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a QuerySet that groups by a column (email) and selects an aggregate (MAX(id) AS m) is used as a subquery in a filter, the compiled subquery should preserve the original grouping semantics. In the example, the subquery used for filter(id=...) should still group by email (GROUP BY U0."email") and return the aggregated value (m) or otherwise produce a semantically equivalent scalar; it should not be transformed into grouping by the primary key (id).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The compiled SQL for the subquery uses GROUP BY on the primary key (id) instead of the original grouping column (email). Example observed subquery fragment: SELECT U0."id" FROM "auth_user" U0 WHERE U0."email" IS NULL GROUP BY U0."id" LIMIT 1 (expected GROUP BY U0."email").

1) Root cause
- In django/db/migrations/serializer.py, EnumSerializer.serialize() serializes enums by serializing their .value and outputting code that reconstructs the enum by calling the enum class with that serialized value:

    v_string, v_imports = serializer_factory(self.value.value).serialize()
    imports = {'import %s' % module, *v_imports}
    return "%s.%s(%s)" % (module, enum_class.__name__, v_string), imports

2) Primary fix
- Change EnumSerializer.serialize() to reference the enum member by name (attribute access), not by value. That avoids serializing/evaluating self.value.value (which may be a Promise) and avoids later breakage when translations change.
- New behavior produces code like module.EnumClass.MEMBER in migration files, which is stable and does not evaluate lazy values.

bug_report.Title: Migrations serialize Enum members using enum value (translatable) instead of member name
bug_report.Description: When an Enum member is used as a default for a CharField, migration serialization uses the Enum member's value (e.g. Status('Good')) rather than a stable reference to the member. If the Enum value is a translatable lazy string (gettext_lazy / Promise), the generated migration file can contain a translated literal; later, when translations change or in other locales, executing the migration raises ValueError because the literal no longer matches any Enum member value.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) EnumSerializer in django/db/migrations/serializer.py serializes enums by serializing the enum member's .value and emitting reconstruction code that calls the enum class with that value (module.EnumClass(value)). This is implemented by calling serializer_factory(self.value.value) and embedding the serialized value into "module.EnumClass(%s)". Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, EnumSerializer.serialize().

2) Serializing the enum member's .value causes evaluation of Promise/gettext_lazy objects when serializer_factory(self.value.value) is used; the evaluated/transformed literal is written into the migration file. Because translated .value is not stable across locales or after translation changes, the migration becomes invalid later. Location (same): django/db/migrations/serializer.py, EnumSerializer.serialize().

3) Tests in tests/migrations/test_writer.py (test_serialize_enums) assert the old constructor-format serialization (e.g. "migrations.test_writer.TextEnum('a-value')" and "migrations.test_writer.IntEnum(2)"). These expectations encode the incorrect assumption that enum members should be serialized by value rather than by stable member reference. Locations: tests/migrations/test_writer.py (tests asserting serialized strings for TextEnum, BinaryEnum, IntEnum).
StepsToReproduce: Define an Enum whose member values are gettext_lazy translations (e.g. Status.GOOD = _('Good')).
Use an Enum member as the default for a CharField in a model (e.g. status = models.CharField(default=Status.GOOD, max_length=128)).
Run makemigrations to generate a migration that includes the default value.
Observe that the generated migration contains code like ("status", models.CharField(default=Status('Good'), ...)).

Change or activate translations (or run in a different locale) so the translation of 'Good' differs; run the migration or import the migration file and observe ValueError: '<translated-string>' is not a valid Status.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The generated migration should refer to the Enum member by a stable code-side reference (e.g. module.Status.MEMBER or module.Status['MEMBER']), not by its value. Migration files should not contain evaluated/translated literals for Enum values, so migrations remain valid regardless of translations or changes to the Enum's .value.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Migrations contain constructor-style references using the Enum member's value (e.g. module.Status('Good')), which embeds the (possibly translated) literal into the migration and can later fail with ValueError when the literal no longer matches any Enum member value.

bug_report.Title: parse_http_date uses hard-coded 0-69/70-99 two-digit year pivot instead of RFC 7231 50-year rule
bug_report.Description: django.utils.http.parse_http_date maps 2-digit years using a hard-coded pivot (0-69 → 2000-2069; 70-99 → 1970-1999). RFC 7231 requires interpreting two-digit years relative to the current year: if the resulting year would be more than 50 years in the future, it must be interpreted as the most recent past year with the same last two digits.
bug_report.RootCause: 1) Hard-coded two-digit year pivot in django/utils/http.py::parse_http_date: years < 100 are mapped by comparing to 70 (if year < 70 → add 2000; else → add 1900). This encodes the incorrect assumption that the mapping is fixed across time. 2) The code does not consult the current year to apply RFC 7231's "more than 50 years in the future" rule. The correct relationship is: for a two-digit year yy, compute candidate = (current_year // 100) * 100 + yy; if candidate - current_year > 50 then candidate -= 100; final year = candidate. Location: django/utils/http.py (function parse_http_date). Current wrong values/formula: year < 70 → year + 2000; year >= 70 → year + 1900. Correct formula: use UTC current year to compute century and apply the >50-years-in-future check as described.
StepsToReproduce: Call django.utils.http.parse_http_date() with an RFC 850 formatted date using a two-digit year, e.g. 'Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT' and observe the returned timestamp/year.

Call django.utils.http.parse_http_date() with an RFC 850 formatted date using a two-digit year that currently falls below the hard-coded pivot, e.g. 'Tue, 04 Jan 37 08:49:37 GMT' (two-digit year '37') and observe the returned year.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Two-digit RFC 850 dates are interpreted relative to the current UTC year: map the two-digit year to the year in the current century that has those last two digits, but if that candidate year is more than 50 years in the future relative to now, interpret it as the most recent past year with the same last two digits.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: parse_http_date maps two-digit years using a fixed pivot: 0-69 → 2000-2069 and 70-99 → 1970-1999, regardless of the current year, violating RFC 7231's 50-year rule.

bug_report.Title: __isnull lookup accepts non-boolean RHS values (should require boolean)
bug_report.Description: The isnull lookup currently accepts arbitrary Python values as its RHS and decides between 'IS NULL' and 'IS NOT NULL' using Python truthiness. This allows non-boolean values (integers, strings, None, etc.) to be used with __isnull, which is undocumented and produces surprising behavior (including interaction with JOIN promotion logic that expects explicit booleans).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) The IsNull lookup implementation in django/db/models/lookups.py encodes the assumption that any truthy/falsy Python value is a valid RHS for __isnull. Location: django/db/models/lookups.py, class IsNull (as_sql uses `if self.rhs:`). This permits non-boolean values (e.g. 1, 0, '', None) and interprets them by Python truthiness.

2) IsNull.prepare_rhs = False and no validation exists for direct RHS values. Location: same class (IsNull.prepare_rhs = False and no get_prep_lookup override). Because prepare_rhs is False the lookup receives raw RHS values and isnull currently never enforces type checking.

3) Query-level code (join promotion) expects an explicit boolean RHS to decide when to require an OUTER JOIN. Location: django/db/models/sql/query.py (code that checks condition.rhs is True to trigger join promotion). The current IsNull behavior of accepting arbitrary truthy/falsy values is inconsistent with that expectation.

Correct relationship / values discovered in investigation:
- The __isnull lookup RHS should be a boolean True or False when passed as a direct Python value. Expressions (objects with resolve_expression) should be allowed to pass through to the query compiler (they are handled differently), but direct non-boolean values must be rejected.
- Current wrong behavior: any truthy value -> treated as True (IS NULL); any falsy value -> treated as False (IS NOT NULL).
- Correct behavior (for direct values): only True -> IS NULL, only False -> IS NOT NULL; other direct values -> raise an error (ValueError).

Files/locations encoding the incorrect assumptions:
- django/db/models/lookups.py: class IsNull (as_sql uses truthiness; no RHS type validation)
- django/db/models/sql/query.py: logic expects condition.rhs to be boolean when deciding JOIN promotion (relies on explicit True/False)
StepsToReproduce: In a Django project shell or view, run Model.objects.filter(some_field__isnull=1) and observe that it executes (treated as truthy) instead of raising an error.

Thought: Summary of investigation and root cause

- The bug: when renaming a PrimaryKey field on a model (ModelA.field_wrong -> field_fixed), Django's migration autodetector generates a RenameField for ModelA but also emits an AlterField for the ForeignKey on the referring model (ModelB) with to_field='field_wrong' — i.e. the ForeignKey's to_field is set to the old name instead of being left implicit (or pointing to the new pk name).

- Root cause: in django/db/migrations/autodetector.py::generate_altered_fields, there's code intended to handle renames of the target model's field_name (the ForeignKey to_field). It detects when the target field was renamed and unconditionally assigns new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name:

    if to_field_rename_key in self.renamed_fields:
        new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name

  This is problematic in the common case where the ForeignKey did not explicitly declare to_field in the source code (it implicitly pointed to the target model's pk). Model rendering / `contribute_to_related_class` may have set remote_field.field_name to the current pk name (new or old) during state rendering. The autodetector's assignment then injects the old pk name (old_field.remote_field.field_name) into new_field.remote_field.field_name, causing deconstruct() to include a to_field kwarg with the old name (since it's different from the new pk) and therefore generating an AlterField that wrongly sets to_field to the old name.

  In short: the autodetector confuses implicit (default-to-pk) ForeignKey references with explicit to_field references and reintroduces the old name where it shouldn't.

Files and locations affected

- Primary location to change:
  - django/db/migrations/autodetector.py, method MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields()

- Why only this location:
  - The logic that causes the to_field to be forced to the old name lives here. The RenameField operation and its state_forwards implementation (which updates remote_field.field_name where appropriate) are correct. The problem arises when autodetector tries to normalize relations for comparison and mistakenly forces an explicit to_field where none was present in the original model definition.

Complete fix (code-level)

Change the logic in generate_altered_fields so that we only override new_field.remote_field.field_name with the old value if the old field actually had an explicit to_field (i.e. it wasn't only the implicit reference to the pk). If the old ForeignKey did not explicitly specify to_field (it was implicitly using the pk), we should not force the old name into new_field.remote_field.field_name — instead we should leave new_field to reference the pk implicitly (i.e. clear remote_field.field_name or leave it as None), which will make deconstruct() avoid emitting to_field and avoid generating the spurious AlterField.

Here is the exact change to make in django/db/migrations/autodetector.py within MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields().

Locate this block (around lines ~918-933 in the copy you inspected):

    # Handle ForeignKey which can only have a single to_field.
    remote_field_name = getattr(new_field.remote_field, 'field_name', None)
    if remote_field_name:
        to_field_rename_key = rename_key + (remote_field_name,)
        if to_field_rename_key in self.renamed_fields:
            new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name

Replace it with (pseudocode patch shown; adjust whitespace/line numbers accordingly):

    # Handle ForeignKey which can only have a single to_field.
    remote_field_name = getattr(new_field.remote_field, 'field_name', None)
    if remote_field_name:
        to_field_rename_key = rename_key + (remote_field_name,)
        if to_field_rename_key in self.renamed_fields:
            # Only preserve an old to_field when the old field explicitly
            # specified a to_field different from its target model's pk.
            # If the old field implicitly referenced the pk (no explicit
            # to_field), don't force the old name into the new field so the
            # new field will continue to use the (renamed) pk implicitly.
            old_remote_field_name = getattr(old_field.remote_field, 'field_name', None)
            old_target_pk_name = None
            if getattr(old_field.remote_field, 'model', None):
                old_target = old_field.remote_field.model
                # old_target may be a string in some states; guard access
                old_target_pk = getattr(getattr(old_target, '_meta', None), 'pk', None)
                if old_target_pk is not None:

bug_report.Title: Autodetector sets ForeignKey.to_field to old PK name when renaming target model's PrimaryKey
bug_report.Description: When renaming a model's primary key field, Django's migration autodetector emits a RenameField for the target model but also generates an AlterField on referring ForeignKeys which sets to_field to the old PK name instead of leaving the FK implicit or pointing to the renamed PK.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/migrations/autodetector.py::MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields(): the autodetector unconditionally copies the old relation field_name into the new field when it detects a to_field rename. The code path is effectively: if to_field_rename_key in self.renamed_fields: new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name. remote_field.field_name corresponds to ForeignKey.to_field. This unconditional assignment treats implicit FK-to-PK references as if they were explicit to_field declarations and forces the old PK name into the new field state. 

2) Because remote_field.field_name is later serialized by Field.deconstruct(), the forced old name (e.g. 'field_wrong') becomes an explicit to_field kwarg in the generated migration, producing an AlterField that pins the FK to the old name. The old value here is old_field.remote_field.field_name (e.g. 'field_wrong'); the correct relationship is that implicit FKs should have remote_field.field_name unset/None (so the FK continues to implicitly refer to the target model's PK after the rename). 

3) The logic that updates the state for an actual RenameField operation (django/db/migrations/operations/fields.RenameField.state_forwards) is correct and updates remote_field.field_name when the remote field explicitly matched the old name. The defect is in the autodetector normalization/compare step that overwrites or reintroduces the old name where no explicit to_field existed. 

4) The intended conditional copy is: only preserve/copy old_field.remote_field.field_name into new_field.remote_field.field_name when the old FK explicitly specified a to_field that was different from the target model's pk. In formula form: if old_remote_field_name is not None and old_remote_field_name != old_target_pk_name then copy old_remote_field_name; otherwise leave new_field.remote_field.field_name unset (None).
StepsToReproduce: Define initial models and create migrations:
class ModelA(models.Model):
field_wrong = models.CharField(max_length=50, primary_key=True)
class ModelB(models.Model):
field_fk = models.ForeignKey(ModelA, blank=True, null=True, on_delete=models.CASCADE)  # no explicit to_field
Run makemigrations/migrate to create and apply initial migration.
Rename the primary key on ModelA:
class ModelA(models.Model):
field_fixed = models.CharField(max_length=50, primary_key=True)
Run makemigrations and inspect the generated migration for ModelB's FK.
Observe that the generated migration contains an AlterField for the FK with to_field='field_wrong' (the old name).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: After renaming ModelA's primary key, makemigrations should generate a RenameField for ModelA. ForeignKeys that did not explicitly declare to_field should remain implicit and not be serialized with a to_field pointing to the old name. No AlterField should be emitted that sets to_field to the previous PK name.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: makemigrations generates a RenameField for ModelA and also emits an AlterField for ModelB's ForeignKey with to_field set to the old primary key name (e.g. to_field='field_wrong'), making the FK explicitly point to the deprecated name.

    references will be resolved relative to `model`.

"""
Accessors for related objects.

When a field defines a relation between two models, each model class provides
an attribute to access related instances of the other model class (unless the
reverse accessor has been disabled with related_name='+').

Accessors are implemented as descriptors in order to customize access and
assignment. This module defines the descriptor classes.

Forward accessors follow foreign keys. Reverse accessors trace them back. For
example, with the following models::

    class Parent(Model):
        pass

    class Child(Model):
        parent = ForeignKey(Parent, related_name='children')

 ``child.parent`` is a forward many-to-one relation. ``parent.children`` is a
reverse many-to-one relation.

There are three types of relations (many-to-one, one-to-one, and many-to-many)
and two directions (forward and reverse) for a total of six combinations.

1. Related instance on the forward side of a many-to-one relation:
   ``ForwardManyToOneDescriptor``.

   Uniqueness of foreign key values is irrelevant to accessing the related
   instance, making the many-to-one and one-to-one cases identical as far as
   the descriptor is concerned. The constraint is checked upstream (unicity
   validation in forms) or downstream (unique indexes in the database).

2. Related instance on the forward side of a one-to-one
   relation: ``ForwardOneToOneDescriptor``.

   It avoids querying the database when accessing the parent link field in
   a multi-table inheritance scenario.

3. Related instance on the reverse side of a one-to-one relation:
   ``ReverseOneToOneDescriptor``.

   One-to-one relations are asymmetrical, despite the apparent symmetry of the
   name, because they're implemented in the database with a foreign key from
   one table to another. As a consequence ``ReverseOneToOneDescriptor`` is
   slightly different from ``ForwardManyToOneDescriptor``.

4. Related objects manager for related instances on the reverse side of a
   many-to-one relation: ``ReverseManyToOneDescriptor``.

   Unlike the previous two classes, this one provides access to a collection
   of objects. It returns a manager rather than an instance.

5. Related objects manager for related instances on the forward or reverse
   sides of a many-to-many relation: ``ManyToManyDescriptor``.

   Many-to-many relations are symmetrical. The syntax of Django models
   requires declaring them on one side but that's an implementation detail.
   They could be declared on the other side without any change in behavior.
   Therefore the forward and reverse descriptors can be the same.

   If you're looking for ``ForwardManyToManyDescriptor`` or
   ``ReverseManyToManyDescriptor``, use ``ManyToManyDescriptor`` instead.
"""

from django.db import connections, router, transaction
from django.db.models import Q, signals
from django.db.models.query import QuerySet
from django.db.models.query_utils import DeferredAttribute
from django.utils.functional import cached_property


class ForeignKeyDeferredAttribute(DeferredAttribute):
    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if instance.__dict__.get(self.field.attname) != value and self.field.is_cached(instance):
            self.field.delete_cached_value(instance)
        instance.__dict__[self.field.attname] = value


class ForwardManyToOneDescriptor:
    """
    Accessor to the related object on the forward side of a many-to-one or
    one-to-one (via ForwardOneToOneDescriptor subclass) relation.

    In the example::

        class Child(Model):
            parent = ForeignKey(Parent, related_name='children')

    ``Child.parent`` is a ``ForwardManyToOneDescriptor`` instance.
    """

    def __init__(self, field_with_rel):
        self.field = field_with_rel

    @cached_property
    def RelatedObjectDoesNotExist(self):
        # The exception can't be created at initialization time since the
        # related model might not be resolved yet; `self.field.model` might
        # still be a string model reference.
        return type(
            'RelatedObjectDoesNotExist',
            (self.field.remote_field.model.DoesNotExist, AttributeError), {
                '__module__': self.field.model.__module__,
                '__qualname__': '%s.%s.RelatedObjectDoesNotExist' % (
                    self.field.model.__qualname__,
                    self.field.name,
                ),
            }
        )

    def is_cached(self, instance):
        return self.field.is_cached(instance)

    def get_queryset(self, **hints):
        return self.field.remote_field.model._base_manager.db_manager(hints=hints).all()

    def get_prefetch_queryset(self, instances, queryset=None):
        if queryset is None:
            queryset = self.get_queryset()
        queryset._add_hints(instance=instances[0])

        rel_obj_attr = self.field.get_foreign_related_value
        instance_attr = self.field.get_local_related_value
        instances_dict = {instance_attr(inst): inst for inst in instances}
        related_field = self.field.foreign_related_fields[0]
        remote_field = self.field.remote_field

        # FIXME: This will need to be revisited when we introduce support for
        # composite fields. In the meantime we take this practical approach to
        # solve a regression on 1.6 when the reverse manager in hidden
        # (related_name ends with a '+'). Refs #21410.
        # The check for len(...) == 1 is a special case that allows the query
        # to be join-less and smaller. Refs #21760.
        if remote_field.is_hidden() or len(self.field.foreign_related_fields) == 1:
            query = {'%s__in' % related_field.name: {instance_attr(inst)[0] for inst in instances}}
        else:
            query = {'%s__in' % self.field.related_query_name(): instances}
        queryset = queryset.filter(**query)

        # Since we're going to assign directly in the cache,
        # we must manage the reverse relation cache manually.
        if not remote_field.multiple:
            for rel_obj in queryset:
                instance = instances_dict[rel_obj_attr(rel_obj)]
                remote_field.set_cached_value(rel_obj, instance)
        return queryset, rel_obj_attr, instance_attr, True, self.field.get_cache_name(), False

    def get_object(self, instance):
        qs = self.get_queryset(instance=instance)
        # Assuming the database enforces foreign keys, this won't fail.
        return qs.get(self.field.get_reverse_related_filter(instance))

        """
        Get the related instance through the forward relation.

        With the example above, when getting ``child.parent``:

        - ``self`` is the descriptor managing the ``parent`` attribute
        - ``instance`` is the ``child`` instance
        - ``cls`` is the ``Child`` class (we don't need it)

            return self

        # The related instance is loaded from the database and then cached
        # by the field on the model instance state. It can also be pre-cached
        # by the reverse accessor (ReverseOneToOneDescriptor).

            rel_obj = self.field.get_cached_value(instance)
        except KeyError:

            ancestor_link = instance._meta.get_ancestor_link(self.field.model) if has_value else None
            if ancestor_link and ancestor_link.is_cached(instance):
                # An ancestor link will exist if this field is defined on a
                # multi-table inheritance parent of the instance's class.
                ancestor = ancestor_link.get_cached_value(instance)
                # The value might be cached on an ancestor if the instance
                # originated from walking down the inheritance chain.
                rel_obj = self.field.get_cached_value(ancestor, default=None)

                remote_field = self.field.remote_field

                # cache on the related object to the current instance to avoid
                # an extra SQL query if it's accessed later on.
                if not remote_field.multiple:

            raise self.RelatedObjectDoesNotExist(

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        """
        Set the related instance through the forward relation.

        With the example above, when setting ``child.parent = parent``:

        - ``self`` is the descriptor managing the ``parent`` attribute
        - ``instance`` is the ``child`` instance
        - ``value`` is the ``parent`` instance on the right of the equal sign

        if value is not None and not isinstance(value, self.field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model):
            raise ValueError(
                'Cannot assign "%r": "%s.%s" must be a "%s" instance.' % (
                    value,
                    instance._meta.object_name,
                    self.field.name,
                    self.field.remote_field.model._meta.object_name,

Thought: Investigation plan
- Extract key entities from the bug report: TextChoices/IntegerChoices, Field attribute getter for CharField/IntegerField, enum.Enum behavior, DeferredAttribute/descriptor/instance assignment.
- Inspect the Choices implementation to understand how enum members are represented.
- Inspect Field and model attribute assignment/descriptors to find where assigned values can be normalized.
- Find the cause of the type mismatch between freshly-created instances (enum.Enum member stored on instance) and instances retrieved from DB (underlying value).
- Propose a complete fix that ensures consistent types for both freshly-created and retrieved instances (i.e., model attributes should store the underlying enum value, not the enum member).

Step 1 — What the bug report shows
- When creating a model instance with a field that has choices defined using TextChoices or IntegerChoices, assigning the enum member directly at creation (MyObject.objects.create(my_str_value=MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE)) leaves the model attribute as the enum member (MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE).
- Reading the same field after retrieving the model from DB (MyObject.objects.last()) yields the underlying value (a str "first" or an int).
- This leads to inconsistent in-memory behavior: a newly-created instance differs in type (enum.Enum) from a fetched-from-db instance (native str/int).

Step 2 — Relevant code paths and findings (what I inspected and why)
- django/db/models/enums.py
  - Read the full file. Choices, IntegerChoices and TextChoices are enum.Enum subclasses; enum members expose `.value` and `.label`. The choices property returns (member.value, member.label). This shows the "DB" value is member.value.
- django/db/models/fields/__init__.py
  - Read Field base class. Notable points:
    - Field.descriptor_class = DeferredAttribute (this is the class used as descriptor at model level).
    - Field.get_prep_value() currently only special-cases Promise objects (does not convert enum.Enum -> .value).
    - Field.contribute_to_class attaches a descriptor instance at the model class using self.descriptor_class(self).
  - Model.__init__ sets attribute values using setattr(self, field.attname, value). Because the descriptor class on the class is DeferredAttribute (which currently only defines __get__), __set__ is not present and thus the attribute assignment writes directly to instance.__dict__ without conversion.
- django/db/models/query_utils.py
  - Found DeferredAttribute: it implements __get__ but not __set__. Because it lacks __set__, attribute assignments on model instances write straight into instance.__dict__.
  - Related descriptors (for ForeignKey) are implemented in django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py and define their own __set__ when necessary; they are not affected by DeferredAttribute changes (they subclass DeferredAttribute and implement __set__ themselves).
- Tests and other references:
  - There is a test helper EnumField used for Postgres tests where get_prep_value converts enum.Enum to .value.
  - There are tests that ensure TextChoices/IntegerChoices work, but existing tests do not assert the type of created instance attribute vs retrieved instance attribute.

Root cause
- Assignment to model attributes for regular fields bypasses any normalization because the descriptor DeferredAttribute lacks a __set__ implementation.
- Model.__init__ (and normal attribute assignment) stores the exact assigned object (enum member) into instance.__dict__, leaving the attribute as an enum.Enum member in-memory.
- When the instance is later retrieved from DB, DB drivers and/or conversion pipeline produce the native Python value (str/int) — so retrieved instances have the expected underlying value type.
- The mismatch comes from:
  - No normalization on assignment (no descriptor __set__ normalization), and
  - Field.get_prep_value not normalizing enum.Enum -> enum.value either (so no central normalization exists to call from descriptor).

Complete fix — Summary
1. Normalize values assigned to model attributes by implementing DeferredAttribute.__set__ so that any assignment to a field attribute is first passed through Field.get_prep_value and only the normalized value is stored on the instance.
2. Extend Field.get_prep_value to convert enum.Enum instances to their underlying .value (so the normalization logic is centralized in the Field API).
3. Add the necessary imports.

Why this is complete:
- Implementing the normalization at DeferredAttribute.__set__ ensures any assignment to descriptor-backed attributes (including assignment during Model.__init__ which uses setattr) will normalize values before they are stored in instance.__dict__.
- Changing Field.get_prep_value ensures the normalization logic is centralized and used across the codebase (and compatible with existing code that already expects get_prep_value to prepare non-Promise values for DB).
- Related-field descriptors (which implement their own __set__) remain unaffected because they are responsible for their own caching and validation semantics, and either already perform appropriate operations or will still function the same — their custom __set__ will continue to be used.

Files that need to change
1. django/db/models/query_utils.py
   - Current behavior: DeferredAttribute defines __get__ but not __set__, so assignments bypass any normalization.
   - Fix: Implement DeferredAttribute.__set__ that stores instance.__dict__[self.field.attname] = self.field.get_prep_value(value).
   - Also add import enum to the top (not strictly necessary here unless we use enum in this file; but we won't rely on enum here — Field.get_prep_value will perform enum handling. Still we do not need enum import in this file; no change required otherwise).

2. django/db/models/fields/__init__.py
   - Current behavior: Field.get_prep_value only converts Promise values using value._proxy____cast(), and otherwise returns the value unchanged.
   - Fix: Extend Field.get_prep_value to convert enum.Enum instances to their underlying .value before returning. Add "import enum" at the top of the file.

Detailed changes (patch-like description)

1) django/db/models/query_utils.py

- Before (excerpt):

      def __get__(self, instance, cls=None):

  - There is no __set__.

- After (excerpt):
  - class DeferredAttribute:
      def __init__(self, field):
          self.field = field
      def __get__(self, instance, cls=None):
          ...
      def __set__(self, instance, value):
          """
          Normalize and store the value for this field on the instance.
          We run the value through the field's get_prep_value so that
          values like enum.Enum members and other types requiring
          normalization are converted to their canonical Python values
          (e.g. enum -> .value) before we store them in instance.__dict__.
          """
          instance.__dict__[self.field.attname] = self.field.get_prep_value(value)

Note about subclasses: Several related descriptors (e.g., ForeignKeyDeferredAttribute) override __set__ (they subclass DeferredAttribute). Python will call the overriding __set__ for them, so their behavior remains as-is.

2) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py

- Import addition at top:
  - import enum

- Change get_prep_value method (excerpt around line ~791):
  - Before:

        """Perform preliminary non-db specific value checks and conversions."""

            value = value._proxy____cast()

  - After:

- DeferredAttribute.__set__ intercepts assignment to any field-backed attribute on model instances (the descriptor is attached to the model class at the attname in Field.contribute_to_class).
  - Model.__init__ uses setattr(self, field.attname, val) to populate the instance; because the descriptor will now have __set__, these assignments will be normalized early, ensuring created instances have the canonical type.
- Field.get_prep_value is the correct place to centralize conversion logic for enum.Enum -> .value, because it's already the method used to prepare values before interacting with DB. Making this conversion in get_prep_value ensures consistency across all code paths that prepare values.
- Related field descriptors that have their own __set__ are not overridden inadvertently (they remain responsible for their own behavior). ForeignKeyDeferredAttribute currently has __set__ and writes directly to instance.__dict__ — this remains behaviorally equivalent; foreign-key assignment semantics (including caching) are independent of this enum->value conversion topic. If a related field wants to normalize enum Enum values on assignment, it can call self.field.get_prep_value itself; that would be a separate change only if needed.

But the bug report demonstrates that this difference is surprising and undesirable for TextChoices/IntegerChoices where one typically expects the stored value to be the native DB type. The normalization is reasonable for the use-case and consistent with DB values.

- Field subclasses that override get_prep_value: many call super().get_prep_value or otherwise process the value. Subclasses that completely replace get_prep_value without calling super() will not get the behavior; but that mirrors current assumptions that such subclasses fully implement normalization themselves. bug_report.Title: Inconsistent in-memory type for TextChoices/IntegerChoices fields: created instance stores Enum member, retrieved instance stores underlying value
bug_report.Description: When a model field uses TextChoices or IntegerChoices for choices, assigning an Enum member at creation time leaves the model attribute as the enum.Enum member in-memory, while retrieving the same row from the database yields the underlying native value (str or int). This causes a type mismatch between newly-created instances and instances loaded from the DB.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Assumption: assigning to a field-backed attribute stores the canonical Python/DB-ready value. Location: Model instance attribute assignment path (Model.__init__ uses setattr(self, field.attname, value)). Reality: assignment bypasses normalization and writes the raw object into instance.__dict__.

2) Missing descriptor behavior: DeferredAttribute (the descriptor attached to ordinary fields) does not implement __set__, so attribute assignment does not run any field-specific normalization. Location: django/db/models/query_utils.py - class DeferredAttribute (no __set__ implemented).

3) Missing centralized normalization for Enum members: Field.get_prep_value does not convert enum.Enum members into their underlying .value. Location: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py - Field.get_prep_value currently only special-cases Promise objects and otherwise returns the value unchanged. Correct relationship: enum.Enum instances represent their canonical storage value via value.value; Field.get_prep_value should return value.value for enum.Enum inputs so that in-memory storage and DB-prepared values are consistent.

4) Combined effect: because (2) prevents conversion on assignment and (3) is the correct method to perform such conversion, freshly-created instances keep the enum.Enum object while instances reconstructed from the DB (which go through DB value conversion/from_db_value) hold the native underlying value (e.g., 'first'), producing the observed mismatch.
StepsToReproduce: Define a TextChoices/IntegerChoices enum, e.g. MyChoice with FIRST_CHOICE = ('first', '...').
Define a model with a CharField/IntegerField using choices=MyChoice.choices (e.g. my_str_value = models.CharField(..., choices=MyChoice.choices)).
Create an instance using the Enum member: my_object = MyObject.objects.create(my_str_value=MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE).
Inspect the created instance attribute: assert isinstance(my_object.my_str_value, str) (this assertion fails).
Retrieve the instance from the DB: my_object2 = MyObject.objects.last(); inspect my_object2.my_str_value which is the native value (str/int).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: For a field whose choices are defined via TextChoices/IntegerChoices, the model attribute should have the same user-visible type (the native underlying value: str for TextChoices, int for IntegerChoices) both immediately after creation and after retrieval from the database. Calling str(...) on the field value of a created instance should yield the same string as on a retrieved instance.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When assigning an Enum member to a field at creation, the created model instance stores and exposes the enum.Enum member (e.g. MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE) in-memory. When the same row is read from the database, the field value is the underlying native type (e.g. 'first'), so type and repr differ between created and retrieved instances (causing assertions like str(value) == 'first' to fail for the created instance).

RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT = 'self'


def resolve_relation(scope_model, relation):
    """
    Transform relation into a model or fully-qualified model string of the form
    "app_label.ModelName", relative to scope_model.

    The relation argument can be:
      * RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT, i.e. the string "self", in which case
        the model argument will be returned.
      * A bare model name without an app_label, in which case scope_model's
        app_label will be prepended.
      * An "app_label.ModelName" string.
      * A model class, which will be returned unchanged.
    """
    # Check for recursive relations
    if relation == RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT:
        relation = scope_model

    # Look for an "app.Model" relation
    if isinstance(relation, str):
        if "." not in relation:
            relation = "%s.%s" % (scope_model._meta.app_label, relation)

    return relation


def lazy_related_operation(function, model, *related_models, **kwargs):
    """
    Schedule `function` to be called once `model` and all `related_models`
    have been imported and registered with the app registry. `function` will
    be called with the newly-loaded model classes as its positional arguments,
    plus any optional keyword arguments.

    The `model` argument must be a model class. Each subsequent positional
    argument is another model, or a reference to another model - see
    `resolve_relation()` for the various forms these may take. Any relative
    references will be resolved relative to `model`.

    This is a convenience wrapper for `Apps.lazy_model_operation` - the app
    registry model used is the one found in `model._meta.apps`.
    """
    models = [model] + [resolve_relation(model, rel) for rel in related_models]
    model_keys = (make_model_tuple(m) for m in models)
    apps = model._meta.apps
    return apps.lazy_model_operation(partial(function, **kwargs), *model_keys)

        arguments that when passed to self.related_field.model.object.filter()

        this field to obj. obj is an instance of self.model.

            for lh_field, rh_field in self.related_fields
        }
        descriptor_filter = self.get_extra_descriptor_filter(obj)

        elif descriptor_filter:

What I found (summary)
- Root cause: Field.contribute_to_class unconditionally creates a get_<field>_display attribute on the model class when a field has choices:

  - Model class creation sequence:
    - ModelBase.__new__ puts non-contributable attributes (i.e. normal user-defined methods) into the new class dict first and collects attributes that have contribute_to_class into contributable_attrs.
    - After the class is created, ModelBase.add_to_class is called for each contributable_attr; that calls value.contribute_to_class(cls, name).
    - Field.contribute_to_class therefore runs after the user's methods have already been attached to the class and unconditionally overwrites any existing attribute named get_<field>_display defined by the user on the class (or defined earlier in inheritance? — see detail below).
- This explains the change the reporter saw: in Django 2.1 this behavior was different (user-defined get_FIELD_display was not overwritten), while in 2.2+ it is overwritten. The repository snapshot here shows the code that overwrites the user method.
- The code uses setattr unconditionally in a few other places where helper methods are dynamically created; similar conflicts may exist there as well.

Historically (and reasonably), we probably want to allow fields to install dynamic methods in case the method is inherited but not defined on the new class. The reported case is a method defined explicitly on the new model, so we must avoid overwriting that. Using cls.__dict__ checks for attributes defined exactly on the class being constructed, which matches the intent: do not overwrite something explicitly defined on this class.

bug_report.Title: Cannot override get_FIELD_display() (model methods overwritten by field/model machinery in Django 2.2+)
bug_report.Description: A model method named get_<field>_display defined on a model class (for example, get_foo_bar_display) is being overwritten during model class construction in Django 2.2+, so user overrides are ignored. The behavior worked in Django 2.1 but in 2.2+ the framework-installed accessor replaces the user-defined method.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py — Field.contribute_to_class: When a Field has choices the code unconditionally calls setattr(cls, 'get_%s_display' % self.name, partialmethod(...)). This unconditionally installs/overwrites get_<field>_display on the class being constructed, thereby destroying any method the author defined on the model class itself. The correct relationship for the accessor installation is: only install the accessor if the class being constructed does not already define that name (i.e., check that 'get_<field>_display' is not present in cls.__dict__).

2) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py — DateField.contribute_to_class: The code unconditionally sets 'get_next_by_<field>' and 'get_previous_by_<field>' via setattr when the field is non-null. These assignments will overwrite user-defined get_next_by_<field>/get_previous_by_<field> methods on the model class. The intended relationship is: only add these accessors when the model class does not already define those names (check target.__dict__).

3) django/db/models/base.py — Model._prepare: The model-preparation code assigns helpers such as get_next_in_order and get_previous_in_order (and applies get_absolute_url overrides from settings) unconditionally. Those assignments can overwrite methods that the model class explicitly defines. The correct behavior is to avoid replacing names defined directly on the class being prepared (i.e., only assign if the name is not in cls.__dict__).

4) django/db/models/base.py — make_foreign_order_accessors: This helper uses setattr to install 'get_<model>_order' and 'set_<model>_order' on the related model without checking whether those names are already defined on the target class. That unconditional install can override explicit methods on the related model; the correct relationship is to only install these accessors when the target class does not already define the given names (check related_model.__dict__).

Rationale about lookup: The observed breakage happens because contribute_to_class runs after the model class has been created and user-defined methods are already on the new class; unguarded setattr therefore overwrites them. Using cls.__dict__ (or target.__dict__) to detect names defined directly on the class preserves explicit user-defined overrides while still allowing dynamic installation when the name is only inherited from a parent class.
StepsToReproduce: Create a Django model with a field that has choices, e.g. foo_bar = models.CharField(choices=[(1, 'foo'), (2, 'bar')]).
Define a method on the model class: def get_foo_bar_display(self): return 'something'.
Create an instance with foo_bar=1 and call instance.get_foo_bar_display() (or call str(instance) if __str__ uses that method).
On Django 2.2+ the call returns the choice label ('foo') instead of the model-defined 'something' (it returns 'something' on Django 2.1).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: If a model class explicitly defines a method named get_<field>_display (or other helper accessors such as get_next_by_<field>, get_previous_by_<field>, get_next_in_order, get_previous_in_order, get_<model>_order, set_<model>_order, or get_absolute_url), that user-defined method should be preserved and invoked. Framework-generated accessors should not silently overwrite methods defined directly on the model class being created.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: During model class construction the field/model code unconditionally sets dynamically-named helper methods (via setattr or direct assignment), overwriting any methods the user defined on that model class. Result: user overrides like get_foo_bar_display() are ignored and the framework-provided accessor (choice label) is returned instead of the user value.
