bug_report.Title: ModelChoiceField ValidationError does not include the invalid value in message
bug_report.Description: When a ModelChoiceField (or a form using it) raises a ValidationError for an invalid choice, the error message is the generic text without showing the offending value. This differs from ChoiceField/MultipleChoiceField, which include the invalid value in the message.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Missing substitution token in ModelChoiceField default message (location: django/forms/models.py, class ModelChoiceField, attribute default_error_messages). Currently: 'Select a valid choice. That choice is not one of the available choices.' This literal message omits the value placeholder. The correct message should include a %(value)s substitution: 'Select a valid choice. %(value)s is not one of the available choices.'

2) ValidationError raised without params in ModelChoiceField.to_python (location: django/forms/models.py, class ModelChoiceField, method to_python). The code raises ValidationError(self.error_messages['invalid_choice'], code='invalid_choice') on ValueError/TypeError/DoesNotExist without passing params={'value': value}. Because the message requires a params mapping to substitute %(value)s, the invalid input is never formatted into the message. The required relationship is: when raising invalid_choice, include params={'value': value} so that '%(value)s' in the message is replaced by the actual invalid input.

3) Test expectations that assert the old literal message (locations: tests/admin_widgets/tests.py - test_nonexistent_target_id, test_invalid_target_id; tests/model_forms/test_modelchoicefield.py - test_basics (c4.id case), test_clean_model_instance, test_disabled_modelchoicefield; tests/model_forms/tests.py - test_validate_related_field_on_default_manager; tests/model_formsets/tests.py - test_validation_with_invalid_id, test_validation_with_nonexistent_id). These tests compare the exact old message text and therefore are inconsistent with the intended behavior (message showing the invalid value). They will need their expected strings updated to include the submitted/invalid value (or to assert the presence of the value and the surrounding message substrings).
StepsToReproduce: Create a ModelChoiceField bound to a model queryset (e.g. f = forms.ModelChoiceField(MyModel.objects.all())).
Pass an invalid value to the field's clean() method (e.g. a pk that is not present in the queryset, or an unrelated model instance).
Observe the raised ValidationError / form.errors message.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When validation fails for an invalid choice, the error message shown to the user includes the invalid value. Example: 'Select a valid choice. 123 is not one of the available choices.' (where '123' is the submitted invalid value).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The error message is a generic text that does not include the invalid value: 'Select a valid choice. That choice is not one of the available choices.'

method_cache.django/db/models/fields/related_descript:
"""
Accessors for related objects.

When a field defines a relation between two models, each model class provides
an attribute to access related instances of the other model class (unless the
reverse accessor has been disabled with related_name='+').

Accessors are implemented as descriptors in order to customize access and
assignment. This module defines the descriptor classes.

Forward accessors follow foreign keys. Reverse accessors trace them back. For
example, with the following models::

    class Parent(Model):
        pass

    class Child(Model):
        parent = ForeignKey(Parent, related_name='children')

 ``child.parent`` is a forward many-to-one relation. ``parent.children`` is a
reverse many-to-one relation.

There are three types of relations (many-to-one, one-to-one, and many-to-many)
and two directions (forward and reverse) for a total of six combinations.

1. Related instance on the forward side of a many-to-one relation:
   ``ForwardManyToOneDescriptor``.

   Uniqueness of foreign key values is irrelevant to accessing the related
   instance, making the many-to-one and one-to-one cases identical as far as
   the descriptor is concerned. The constraint is checked upstream (unicity
   validation in forms) or downstream (unique indexes in the database).

2. Related instance on the forward side of a one-to-one
   relation: ``ForwardOneToOneDescriptor``.

   It avoids querying the database when accessing the parent link field in
   a multi-table inheritance scenario.

3. Related instance on the reverse side of a one-to-one relation:
   ``ReverseOneToOneDescriptor``.

   One-to-one relations are asymmetrical, despite the apparent symmetry of the
   name, because they're implemented in the database with a foreign key from
   one table to another. As a consequence ``ReverseOneToOneDescriptor`` is
   slightly different from ``ForwardManyToOneDescriptor``.

4. Related objects manager for related instances on the reverse side of a
   many-to-one relation: ``ReverseManyToOneDescriptor``.

   Unlike the previous two classes, this one provides access to a collection
   of objects. It returns a manager rather than an instance.

5. Related objects manager for related instances on the forward or reverse
   sides of a many-to-many relation: ``ManyToManyDescriptor``.

   Many-to-many relations are symmetrical. The syntax of Django models
   requires declaring them on one side but that's an implementation detail.
   They could be declared on the other side without any change in behavior.
   Therefore the forward and reverse descriptors can be the same.

   If you're looking for ``ForwardManyToManyDescriptor`` or
   ``ReverseManyToManyDescriptor``, use ``ManyToManyDescriptor`` instead.
"""

from django.core.exceptions import FieldError
from django.db import connections, router, transaction
from django.db.models import Q, signals
from django.db.models.query import QuerySet
from django.db.models.query_utils import DeferredAttribute
from django.db.models.utils import resolve_callables
from django.utils.functional import cached_property


class ForeignKeyDeferredAttribute(DeferredAttribute):
    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if instance.__dict__.get(self.field.attname) != value and self.field.is_cached(instance):
            self.field.delete_cached_value(instance)
        instance.__dict__[self.field.attname] = value


class ForwardManyToOneDescriptor:
    """
    Accessor to the related object on the forward side of a many-to-one or
    one-to-one (via ForwardOneToOneDescriptor subclass) relation.

    In the example::

        class Child(Model):
            parent = ForeignKey(Parent, related_name='children')

    ``Child.parent`` is a ``ForwardManyToOneDescriptor`` instance.
    """

    def __init__(self, field_with_rel):
        self.field = field_with_rel

    @cached_property
    def RelatedObjectDoesNotExist(self):
        # The exception can't be created at initialization time since the
        # related model might not be resolved yet; `self.field.model` might
        # still be a string model reference.
        return type(
            'RelatedObjectDoesNotExist',
            (self.field.remote_field.model.DoesNotExist, AttributeError), {
                '__module__': self.field.model.__module__,
                '__qualname__': '%s.%s.RelatedObjectDoesNotExist' % (
                    self.field.model.__qualname__,
                    self.field.name,
                ),
            }
        )

    def is_cached(self, instance):
        return self.field.is_cached(instance)

    def get_queryset(self, **hints):
        return self.field.remote_field.model._base_manager.db_manager(hints=hints).all()

    def get_prefetch_queryset(self, instances, queryset=None):
        if queryset is None:
            queryset = self.get_queryset()
        queryset._add_hints(instance=instances[0])

        rel_obj_attr = self.field.get_foreign_related_value
        instance_attr = self.field.get_local_related_value
        instances_dict = {instance_attr(inst): inst for inst in instances}
        related_field = self.field.foreign_related_fields[0]
        remote_field = self.field.remote_field

        # FIXME: This will need to be revisited when we introduce support for
        # composite fields. In the meantime we take this practical approach to
        # solve a regression on 1.6 when the reverse manager in hidden
        # (related_name ends with a '+'). Refs #21410.
        # The check for len(...) == 1 is a special case that allows the query
        # to be join-less and smaller. Refs #21760.
        if remote_field.is_hidden() or len(self.field.foreign_related_fields) == 1:
            query = {'%s__in' % related_field.name: {instance_attr(inst)[0] for inst in instances}}
        else:
            query = {'%s__in' % self.field.related_query_name(): instances}
        queryset = queryset.filter(**query)

        # Since we're going to assign directly in the cache,
        # we must manage the reverse relation cache manually.
        if not remote_field.multiple:
            for rel_obj in queryset:
                instance = instances_dict[rel_obj_attr(rel_obj)]
                remote_field.set_cached_value(rel_obj, instance)
        return queryset, rel_obj_attr, instance_attr, True, self.field.get_cache_name(), False

    def get_object(self, instance):
        qs = self.get_queryset(instance=instance)
        # Assuming the database enforces foreign keys, this won't fail.
        return qs.get(self.field.get_reverse_related_filter(instance))

    def __get__(self, instance, cls=None):
        """
        Get the related instance through the forward relation.

        With the example above, when getting ``child.parent``:

        - ``self`` is the descriptor managing the ``parent`` attribute
        - ``instance`` is the ``child`` instance
        - ``cls`` is the ``Child`` class (we don't need it)
        """
        if instance is None:
            return self

        # The related instance is loaded from the database and then cached
        # by the field on the model instance state. It can also be pre-cached
        # by the reverse accessor (ReverseOneToOneDescriptor).
        try:
            rel_obj = self.field.get_cached_value(instance)
        except KeyError:
            has_value = None not in self.field.get_local_related_value(instance)
            ancestor_link = instance._meta.get_ancestor_link(self.field.model) if has_value else None
            if ancestor_link and ancestor_link.is_cached(instance):
                # An ancestor link will exist if this field is defined on a
                # multi-table inheritance parent of the instance's class.
                ancestor = ancestor_link.get_cached_value(instance)
                # The value might be cached on an ancestor if the instance
                # originated from walking down the inheritance chain.
                rel_obj = self.field.get_cached_value(ancestor, default=None)
            else:
                rel_obj = None
            if rel_obj is None and has_value:
                rel_obj = self.get_object(instance)
                remote_field = self.field.remote_field
                # If this is a one-to-one relation, set the reverse accessor
                # cache on the related object to the current instance to avoid
                # an extra SQL query if it's accessed later on.
                if not remote_field.multiple:
                    remote_field.set_cached_value(rel_obj, instance)
            self.field.set_cached_value(instance, rel_obj)

        if rel_obj is None and not self.field.null:
            raise self.RelatedObjectDoesNotExist(
                "%s has no %s." % (self.field.model.__name__, self.field.name)
            )
        else:
            return rel_obj

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        """
        Set the related instance through the forward relation.

        With the example above, when setting ``child.parent = parent``:

        - ``self`` is the descriptor managing the ``parent`` attribute
        - ``instance`` is the ``child`` instance
        - ``value`` is the ``parent`` instance on the right of the equal sign
        """
        # An object must be an instance of the related class.
        if value is not None and not isinstance(value, self.field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model):
            raise ValueError(
                'Cannot assign "%r": "%s.%s" must be a "%s" instance.' % (
                    value,
                    instance._meta.object_name,
                    self.field.name,
                    self.field.remote_field.model._meta.object_name,
                )
            )
        elif value is not None:
            if instance._state.db is None:
                instance._state.db = router.db_for_write(instance.__class__, instance=value)
            if value._state.db is None:
                value._state.db = router.db_for_write(value.__class__, instance=instance)
            if not router.allow_relation(value, instance):
                raise ValueError('Cannot assign "%r": the current database router prevents this relation.' % value)

        remote_field = self.field.remote_field
        # If we're setting the value of a OneToOneField to None, we need to clear
        # out the cache on any old related object. Otherwise, deleting the
        # previously-related object will also cause this object to be deleted,
        # which is wrong.
        if value is None:
            # Look up the previously-related object, which may still be available
            # since we've not yet cleared out the related field.
            # Use the cache directly, instead of the accessor; if we haven't
            # populated the cache, then we don't care - we're only accessing
            # the object to invalidate the accessor cache, so there's no
            # need to populate the cache just to expire it again.
            related = self.field.get_cached_value(instance, default=None)

            # If we've got an old related object, we need to clear out its
            # cache. This cache also might not exist if the related object
            # hasn't been accessed yet.
            if related is not None:
                remote_field.set_cached_value(related, None)

            for lh_field, rh_field in self.field.related_fields:
                setattr(instance, lh_field.attname, None)

        # Set the values of the related field.
        else:
            for lh_field, rh_field in self.field.related_fields:
                setattr(instance, lh_field.attname, getattr(value, rh_field.attname))

bug_report.Title: Assigning unsaved related instance with non-numeric PK leaves parent's FK as empty string and prevents later update
bug_report.Description: When a parent model's ForeignKey is assigned an unsaved related instance whose primary key is a non-auto CharField, the parent's local foreign-key column is set to an empty string at assignment time and is not updated when the related instance's PK is later defined and saved. This leads to the parent persisting an empty-string FK (and a deferred DB FK violation on commit) instead of the related instance's PK.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect eager copy in the forward relation descriptor: django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py -> ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__set__ directly sets the parent's local FK attribute from the related object's corresponding attribute using
   setattr(instance, lh_field.attname, getattr(value, rh_field.attname)).
   This copies the raw related-field attribute value at assignment time.

2) Incompatible semantics for non-auto CharField primary keys: For an unsaved related instance whose PK is a CharField with the default empty-string value, getattr(value, rh_field.attname) returns "" (empty string). That value is copied into the parent's local FK attribute at assignment time (see item 1).

3) Existing save-time recovery requires parent's FK to be None: django/db/models/base.py -> Model._prepare_related_fields_for_save() only repopulates the parent's local FK from the cached related object when getattr(self, field.attname) is None (it uses obj.pk to populate the parent's field). Because the forward-descriptor copied "" (not None) at assignment time, the save-time logic does not run and the parent's FK remains the empty string.

4) Different behavior for auto-increment numeric PKs: For related instances with auto/integer PKs, the related attribute is None before save, so the descriptor sets the parent's FK attribute to None and Model._prepare_related_fields_for_save() correctly fills it from obj.pk after the related instance is saved. The descriptor's current behavior therefore creates a conditional difference between auto PKs (works) and non-auto CharField PKs (fails).
StepsToReproduce: Start a transaction (transaction.atomic()).
Create parent instance: order = Order()
Assign an unsaved related instance without a PK: order.product = Product()
Set the related instance's primary key and save it: order.product.sku = 'foo'; order.product.save()
Save the parent: order.save()
Observe that the parent's product_id was persisted as an empty string and that a deferred foreign key constraint causes failure on transaction commit.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: After assigning an unsaved related instance and later setting and saving that related instance's primary key, saving the parent should persist the parent's foreign-key column equal to the related instance's final primary key (e.g., product_id == 'foo'). Assignment of an unsaved related instance should not permanently freeze the parent's FK to the related field's empty-string default.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When assigning an unsaved related Product() whose PK is a CharField with default empty string, the parent's product_id is immediately set to "" and remains "" after the related instance is given a pk and saved; the parent save persists an empty string and the transaction later fails with a foreign key violation.

"""
A class for storing a tree graph. Primarily used for filter constructs in the
ORM.
"""

import copy

from django.utils.hashable import make_hashable


class Node:
    """
    A single internal node in the tree graph. A Node should be viewed as a
    connection (the root) with the children being either leaf nodes or other
    Node instances.
    """
    # Standard connector type. Clients usually won't use this at all and
    # subclasses will usually override the value.
    default = 'DEFAULT'

    def __init__(self, children=None, connector=None, negated=False):
        """Construct a new Node. If no connector is given, use the default."""
        self.children = children[:] if children else []
        self.connector = connector or self.default
        self.negated = negated

    # Required because django.db.models.query_utils.Q. Q. __init__() is
    # problematic, but it is a natural Node subclass in all other respects.
    @classmethod
    def _new_instance(cls, children=None, connector=None, negated=False):
        """
        Create a new instance of this class when new Nodes (or subclasses) are
        needed in the internal code in this class. Normally, it just shadows
        __init__(). However, subclasses with an __init__ signature that aren't
        an extension of Node.__init__ might need to implement this method to
        allow a Node to create a new instance of them (if they have any extra
        setting up to do).
        """
        obj = Node(children, connector, negated)
        obj.__class__ = cls
        return obj

    def __str__(self):
        template = '(NOT (%s: %s))' if self.negated else '(%s: %s)'
        return template % (self.connector, ', '.join(str(c) for c in self.children))

    def __repr__(self):
        return "<%s: %s>" % (self.__class__.__name__, self)

    def __deepcopy__(self, memodict):
        obj = Node(connector=self.connector, negated=self.negated)
        obj.__class__ = self.__class__
        obj.children = copy.deepcopy(self.children, memodict)
        return obj

    def __len__(self):
        """Return the number of children this node has."""
        return len(self.children)

    def __bool__(self):
        """Return whether or not this node has children."""
        return bool(self.children)

    def __contains__(self, other):
        """Return True if 'other' is a direct child of this instance."""
        return other in self.children

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return (
            self.__class__ == other.__class__ and
            (self.connector, self.negated) == (other.connector, other.negated) and
            self.children == other.children
        )

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.__class__, self.connector, self.negated, *make_hashable(self.children)))

    def add(self, data, conn_type, squash=True):
        """
        Combine this tree and the data represented by data using the
        connector conn_type. The combine is done by squashing the node other
        away if possible.

        This tree (self) will never be pushed to a child node of the
        combined tree, nor will the connector or negated properties change.

        Return a node which can be used in place of data regardless if the
        node other got squashed or not.

        If `squash` is False the data is prepared and added as a child to
        this tree without further logic.
        """
        if data in self.children:
            return data
        if not squash:
            self.children.append(data)
            return data
        if self.connector == conn_type:
            # We can reuse self.children to append or squash the node other.
            if (isinstance(data, Node) and not data.negated and
                    (data.connector == conn_type or len(data) == 1)):
                # We can squash the other node's children directly into this
                # node. We are just doing (AB)(CD) == (ABCD) here, with the
                # addition that if the length of the other node is 1 the
                # connector doesn't matter. However, for the len(self) == 1
                # case we don't want to do the squashing, as it would alter
                # self.connector.
                self.children.extend(data.children)
                return self
            else:
                # We could use perhaps additional logic here to see if some
                # children could be used for pushdown here.
                self.children.append(data)
                return data
        else:
            obj = self._new_instance(self.children, self.connector,
                                     self.negated)
            self.connector = conn_type
            self.children = [obj, data]
            return data

    def negate(self):
        """Negate the sense of the root connector."""
        self.negated = not self.negated

Thought: Reasoning / plan
- The bug involves Q() | Q(x__in={}.keys()) failing with TypeError: cannot pickle 'dict_keys' object.
- Q is a subclass of django.utils.tree.Node. Q._combine uses copy.deepcopy(self) when one side is empty, which delegates to Node.__deepcopy__.
- I inspected Node.__deepcopy__ (django/utils/tree.py) and found it calls copy.deepcopy(self.children, memodict). copy.deepcopy on elements like dict_keys can fail because dict_keys objects are not picklable, which can cause deepcopy to raise TypeError (via pickle) during the deepcopy operation.
- The proper fix is to make Node.__deepcopy__ robust to children that cannot be deep-copied: attempt deep copy per child, but if that fails, fall back to a shallow copy of that child (so we still produce a new Node object rather than raising during combination).
- Q._combine itself is fine to keep using copy.deepcopy; the fix is centralized in Node.__deepcopy__ so all Node subclasses (including Q) get robust deepcopy behavior.

What I changed
1) File: django/utils/tree.py
- Current code for Node.__deepcopy__ (simplified):
  obj = Node(connector=self.connector, negated=self.negated)
  obj.__class__ = self.__class__
  obj.children = copy.deepcopy(self.children, memodict)
  return obj

- Problem: copy.deepcopy(self.children, memodict) may raise TypeError when encountering elements that are not deepcopy-able/picklable (e.g. dict_keys on Python 3), causing operations like Q() | Q(x__in={}.keys()) to raise.

- Fix: deep-copy children individually, and for each child, if copy.deepcopy(child, memodict) raises TypeError, fall back to using the original child (shallow copy). This preserves the behavior of returning a new Node instance but avoids crashing on unpickleable/deepcopy-unfriendly objects contained in children.

Proposed patch (complete updated method)
Replace Node.__deepcopy__ in django/utils/tree.py with:

def __deepcopy__(self, memodict):
    obj = Node(connector=self.connector, negated=self.negated)
    obj.__class__ = self.__class__
    new_children = []
    for child in self.children:
        try:
            new_children.append(copy.deepcopy(child, memodict))
        except TypeError:
            # Some objects (e.g. dict_keys) cannot be deep-copied/pickled;
            # fall back to a shallow copy of the child to avoid failing
            # Q combination or other Node deepcopy operations.
            new_children.append(child)
    obj.children = new_children
    return obj

Rationale and considerations
- This fix centralizes the behavior in Node.__deepcopy__, which is appropriate because Node is the base class for Q and other tree-like objects. It ensures other code paths that deep-copy Nodes (or Qs) won't fail on unpickleable child values.
- Falling back to a shallow copy for problematic children is a pragmatic choice:
  - Deep copying is used in these cases to avoid mutating the original when combining nodes; returning the original child as-is keeps referential semantics for the child but still returns a new Node object (so changing the Node's children list doesn't mutate the original Node).
  - Alternative would be to try to coerce certain container views (like dict_keys) into concrete types (e.g. list) automatically. That could be surprising: it would change the type of the child value rather than just avoiding an exception. The approach in this patch is conservative and non-breaking.
- The only other place relevant is Q._combine (django/db/models/query_utils.py), which uses copy.deepcopy(self) / copy.deepcopy(other). After this change the deepcopy calls will use the updated Node.__deepcopy__, so the operation will no longer raise for dict_keys children. No change is required in Q._combine itself.

Other affected locations to be aware of
- django/db/models/query_utils.py (Q._combine): uses copy.deepcopy and is the trigger site for the bug, but it should remain unchanged. The fix is in Node.__deepcopy__ so Q._combine gets robust behavior automatically.
- There are many other copy.deepcopy usages in the codebase. The pattern used here (try deepcopy and on TypeError fall back to shallow copy) could be considered for other places where copying structures may include non-deepcopyable objects, but applying it globally is not safe without reviewing each usage. For the current bug, changing Node.__deepcopy__ is the correct minimal, complete fix.

- Using copy.copy would produce a shallow copy of the Node itself (and its children list would still reference same child objects and the same list unless you specifically make shallow copies of internal structures). That risks subtle shared-state bugs if callers expect independent Node objects after combining. It is better to keep deepcopy semantics and make deepcopy resilient to unpickleable children.

Complete patch summary
- Modify django/utils/tree.py Node.__deepcopy__ as shown above to try copy.deepcopy per child and fall back to the original child on TypeError.

bug_report.Title: TypeError: cannot pickle 'dict_keys' when combining Q objects with | operator
bug_report.Description: Applying the | operator to combine Q() with a Q that contains a non-deepcopyable child (e.g. dict_keys from {}.keys()) raises TypeError: cannot pickle 'dict_keys' object. The error occurs during the internal deepcopy used when combining Q objects.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/utils/tree.py:Node.__deepcopy__ assumes the entire children sequence can be deep-copied in one call. It sets obj.children = copy.deepcopy(self.children, memodict). This fails when a child value is not deepcopy/pickle-able (example: dict_keys on Python 3), raising TypeError: cannot pickle 'dict_keys' object.
2) django/db/models/query_utils.py:Q._combine relies on copy.deepcopy(self) / copy.deepcopy(other) when one side is empty. That triggers Node.__deepcopy__ and thus exposes the failure in (1) when combining Q objects that contain non-deepcopyable children.
3) Incorrect assumption: Node implementations (and callers such as Q._combine) assume all child values are deepcopy-able/pickle-able. In reality some common Python objects (e.g. dict_keys) are not, so deep-copying children must tolerate per-child deepcopy failures. The correct relationship for Node.__deepcopy__ is to produce a new Node whose children are obtained by attempting deepcopy on each child individually and, if deepcopy(child, memodict) raises TypeError, falling back to the original child (shallow) so that combining nodes does not raise.
StepsToReproduce: python -c "from django.db.models import Q; a = Q(); b = Q(x__in={}.keys()); print(b); print(a | b)"
Or interactively:
>>> from django.db.models import Q
>>> Q() | Q(x__in={}.keys())  # raises TypeError: cannot pickle 'dict_keys' object

The result should be a Q object representing the combined query; child values such as dict_keys should be preserved as child values (visible in repr) and should not cause a TypeError during combination.

Thought: Plan / starting point
- The report implicates Q.__and__ / Q._combine and the Exists expression. The bug is that Q() & Exists(...) raises TypeError while Exists(...) & Q() works. I need to inspect Q (query_utils.py) and Exists / Expression / Combinable (expressions.py) to see how operator fallback should work.

What I looked for and why
1. Opened django/db/models/query_utils.py to read the full Q class (to inspect _combine, __and__, __or__, ...). This is where the TypeError originates (as shown in the stacktrace).
2. Opened django/db/models/expressions.py to inspect Expression / Combinable and the Exists class (to check how reversed operators are handled for expressions).
3. Searched for other implementations of __rand__/__ror__ to find precedent (postgres search classes implement reverse operators in a similar style).
4. Reviewed Combinable (base for Expression) operator implementations to understand expectations.

Findings (analysis)
- Q._combine currently starts with:
    if not isinstance(other, Q):
        raise TypeError(other)

  That raises a TypeError immediately whenever the right operand is not a Q instance. In Python's binary operator resolution for a & b:
  - It first calls a.__and__(b). If that returns NotImplemented, Python then tries b.__rand__(a). But if a.__and__ raises an exception (TypeError), Python will not try the right operand: exception propagates.

- Exists is an expression that inherits from Subquery -> Expression, and Expression mixes in Combinable. Combinable defines __and__/__or__ for expressions (they create Q(self) & Q(other) when both operands are conditional), but Combinable.__rand__ and __ror__ are currently implemented to raise NotImplementedError. That means even if Q.__and__ returned NotImplemented, the right-hand side's __rand__ presently raises NotImplementedError (raising an exception), preventing normal fallback behavior.

- The combination Exists(...) & Q() works because it calls Exists.__and__(Q()), and Combinable.__and__ checks conditional and then returns Q(self) & Q(other) (both are conditional), so that path succeeds.

- The failing case Q() & Exists(...) calls Q.__and__(Exists). Q._combine raises TypeError(Exists) and so Python does not attempt Exists.__rand__; it just errors out.

Root cause
- Two cooperating problems:
  1. Q._combine raises TypeError when the other operand is not a Q. That prevents Python from trying the reversed operator on the right-hand side.
  2. Combinable.__rand__/__ror__ raise NotImplementedError instead of implementing the reversed boolean combination for Q objects (or returning NotImplemented so Python can continue). Even if Q._combine returned NotImplemented, Combinable.__rand__/__ror__ raising NotImplementedError would produce an exception instead of a graceful fallback.

Fix — complete set of changes required
We need two changes so the & and | operators are commutative between Q and conditional Expressions (like Exists):

1) django/db/models/query_utils.py (Q._combine)
- Current behavior:
    if not isinstance(other, Q):
        raise TypeError(other)

- Problem: raising TypeError blocks operator fallback (right operand's __rand__/__ror__).

- Fix: return NotImplemented when other is not a Q instance. This signals Python to try the reflected operation (other.__rand__/__ror__) instead.

- Change to:
    if not isinstance(other, Q):
        return NotImplemented

Location: Q._combine in django/db/models/query_utils.py.

Rationale: the special value NotImplemented is the standard protocol to allow Python to call the reflected operator on the other operand. Returning NotImplemented is the correct behavior for unsupported operand types, rather than immediately raising.

Side effects: The exact TypeError message for expressions like Q() & 1 will change (Python will raise the generic unsupported operand types TypeError if the reflected operation doesn't handle it), which is the correct and expected Python behaviour.

2) django/db/models/expressions.py (Combinable.__rand__ and Combinable.__ror__)
- Current behavior (excerpt):
    def __rand__(self, other):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "Use .bitand() and .bitor() for bitwise logical operations."
        )

    def __ror__(self, other):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "Use .bitand() and .bitor() for bitwise logical operations."
        )

- Problem: When Q._combine returns NotImplemented and Python attempts Exists.__rand__(Q), __rand__ raises NotImplementedError, causing an exception instead of allowing proper combination logic.

- Fix: Implement __rand__ and __ror__ to support reversed boolean combination with Q instances. The reversed method should:
    - If both operands are conditional (have .conditional True), return Q(other) & Q(self) or Q(other) | Q(self), respectively (or simply return other & Q(self) if other is a Q).
    - Otherwise return NotImplemented to allow Python to continue with other fallback behavior.

- Proposed code changes:

Replace __rand__ with:

    def __rand__(self, other):
        # Support reversed boolean combination with Q objects.
        if getattr(self, 'conditional', False) and getattr(other, 'conditional', False):
            # other is expected to be a Q instance in reversed operations
            return Q(other) & Q(self)
        return NotImplemented

Replace __ror__ with:

    def __ror__(self, other):
        if getattr(self, 'conditional', False) and getattr(other, 'conditional', False):
            return Q(other) | Q(self)
        return NotImplemented

Location: class Combinable in django/db/models/expressions.py (methods __rand__ and __ror__).

Rationale: This mirrors how Combinable.__and__ and __or__ behave for left-side expression combinations, and lets reversed combos like Q() & Exists(...) succeed by letting the right-side expression assemble a combined Q object. Returning NotImplemented when not applicable follows Python protocol.

Testing additions recommended
- Add unit tests to assert symmetry of boolean operators between Q and conditional Expressions (Exists, and perhaps other boolean expressions):

Example tests:
- qs = Product.objects.all()
- assert isinstance(Exists(qs) & Q(), Q)
- assert isinstance(Q() & Exists(qs), Q)
- assert isinstance(Q() | Exists(qs), Q)
- assert isinstance(Exists(qs) | Q(), Q)
- (Edge case) ensure Q() & 1 raises TypeError, not a different exception.

Concrete diffs (what to change)

1) django/db/models/query_utils.py
- Replace the early TypeError raise in _combine:

Original:
    def _combine(self, other, conn):
        if not isinstance(other, Q):
            raise TypeError(other)

Proposed:
    def _combine(self, other, conn):
        if not isinstance(other, Q):
            # Allow Python to call other's __rand__/__ror__ for reversed operands.
            return NotImplemented

2) django/db/models/expressions.py
- Replace __rand__ and __ror__ implementations in Combinable:

Original:
    def __rand__(self, other):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "Use .bitand() and .bitor() for bitwise logical operations."
        )

    def __ror__(self, other):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "Use .bitand() and .bitor() for bitwise logical operations."
        )

Proposed:
    def __rand__(self, other):
        # Support reversed boolean combination with Q objects.
        if getattr(self, 'conditional', False) and getattr(other, 'conditional', False):
            return Q(other) & Q(self)
        return NotImplemented

    def __ror__(self, other):
        if getattr(self, 'conditional', False) and getattr(other, 'conditional', False):
            return Q(other) | Q(self)
        return NotImplemented

(Notes: expressions.py already imports Q from django.db.models.query_utils at the top, so Q is available.)

Why this is a complete fix
- The original error arises from Q refusing non-Q values (raising TypeError) rather than deferring to reversed operator. Changing Q._combine to return NotImplemented uses the Python protocol for binary operations and gives the other operand a chance.
- The other operand (an Expression / Combinable) needs to participate in the reversed operation. Implementing __rand__/__ror__ to handle Q on the left (and to otherwise return NotImplemented) ensures the symmetric behavior between Q and Expression boolean operations.
- Both files changed are the only places that need modification for this specific behavior:
  - Q._combine is where Q blocks reversed operations.
  - Combinable.__rand__/__ror__ are the natural place to implement reversed operator behavior for Expression subclasses (Exists is a Subquery -> Expression).

Potential side-effects and compatibility
- The TypeError messaging for cases like Q() & 1 will differ (Python's generic "unsupported operand types" vs the older TypeError(other) message). Returning NotImplemented and properly using the reflected operator is the correct Python behavior and gives a consistent result (TypeError) for truly unsupported combinations.
- There are no backwards-incompatible changes to behavior of valid combinations (the fix only makes previously failing valid combinations succeed in the symmetric order).

Suggested tests to add
- Tests asserting commutativity of & and | between Q and conditional Expression types (Exists is the obvious candidate).
- Tests that unsupported operand combinations still raise TypeError (but maybe not test the exact message).

Summary (short)
- Root cause: Q._combine raises TypeError for non-Q operands instead of returning NotImplemented; and Combinable.__rand__/__ror__ raise NotImplementedError instead of implementing symmetric boolean combination semantics. This prevents Python from trying the reflected operator and results in a TypeError when swapping operand order.
- Fix: Q._combine should return NotImplemented when other is not a Q (so Python tries other's __rand__/__ror__), and Combinable.__rand__/__ror__ should implement reversed boolean combination with Q (or return NotImplemented if not applicable).
- Files to change:
  - django/db/models/query_utils.py: Q._combine: raise -> return NotImplemented
  - django/db/models/expressions.py: Combinable.__rand__ and __ror__: implement reversed Q combination (return Q(other) & Q(self) / Q(other) | Q(self)) or return NotImplemented.

If you want, I can produce the exact patch (unified diff) for these two files.

bug_report.Title: Q & Exists ordering not commutative: Q() & Exists(...) raises TypeError
bug_report.Description: Combining a Q() object with an Exists(...) expression using & (and |) is not commutative. Exists(...) & Q() succeeds, but Q() & Exists(...) raises a TypeError and aborts instead of allowing the reflected operator to run.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Q._combine in django/db/models/query_utils.py raises TypeError(other) when the right-hand operand is not a Q instance. Location: class Q, method _combine (django/db/models/query_utils.py). Incorrect assumption: that raising TypeError is the correct way to indicate an unsupported operand. Correct relationship/protocol: when the left operand does not handle the operation for the given other type, the method should return NotImplemented so Python will try the right operand's reflected operator (__rand__/__ror__).

2) Combinable.__rand__ and Combinable.__ror__ in django/db/models/expressions.py unconditionally raise NotImplementedError. Location: class Combinable, methods __rand__ and __ror__ (django/db/models/expressions.py). Incorrect assumption: reversed boolean combination is not supported and should raise a NotImplementedError. Correct relationship/behavior for conditional expressions (like Exists, which inherit Combinable/Expression): when a reversed boolean operator is invoked with a Q on the left, the reversed method should return a combined Q object (the investigated formula is Q(other) & Q(self) for &, and Q(other) | Q(self) for |) when both operands are conditional; otherwise it should return NotImplemented so Python can continue fallback behavior.
StepsToReproduce: Open a Django shell with the project models loaded.
In [1]: from django.db.models import Q, Exists
In [2]: qs = Product.objects.all()
In [3]: Exists(qs) & Q()   # works
In [4]: Q() & Exists(qs)   # raises TypeError
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The bitwise boolean operators (& and |) are commutative between Q objects and conditional Expression objects (like Exists). Both Q() & Exists(...) and Exists(...) & Q() should succeed and produce a combined Q object representing the composed condition (visible as a <Q: ...> representation).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Exists(Product.objects.all()) & Q() returns a combined Q object. Q() & Exists(Product.objects.all()) raises a TypeError with the non-Q operand printed (e.g. TypeError: <django.db.models.expressions.Exists object at 0x...>), and a traceback showing the exception raised from Q._combine in django/db/models/query_utils.py.

bug_report.Title: ResolverMatch.__repr__ shows 'functools.partial' and hides partial-provided args/kwargs
bug_report.Description: When a functools.partial object is used as the resolved view callback, ResolverMatch.__repr__ prints the callback as 'functools.partial' and does not expose the positional/keyword arguments that were bound into the partial. This makes the representation unhelpful for debugging and hides the actual underlying function and pre-specified arguments.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) ResolverMatch.__init__ stores the passed func object directly in self.func and computes self._func_path from hasattr(func, '__name__'). This treats functools.partial instances like any other callable; partial has no __name__, so _func_path becomes 'functools.partial' (file: django/urls/resolvers.py, class ResolverMatch, method __init__).

2) ResolverMatch.__init__ does not merge functools.partial pre-specified positional args (partial.args) and keyword arguments (partial.keywords) into the ResolverMatch.args / ResolverMatch.kwargs. As a result, __repr__ prints only the URL-captured args/kwargs and not the effective call arguments (file: django/urls/resolvers.py, class ResolverMatch, method __init__).

3) The correct relationships discovered in the investigation that must be preserved in the diagnosis:
   - If func is a functools.partial, the effective positional arguments passed to the underlying callable are partial.args followed by the URL-captured args (i.e. effective_args = tuple(partial.args) + tuple(url_args)).
   - If func is a functools.partial, the effective keyword arguments are partial.keywords updated by URL-captured kwargs with URL-captured kwargs taking precedence (i.e. effective_kwargs = {**(partial.keywords or {}), **(url_kwargs or {})}).
   - For representation of the callable path, the underlying callable (partial.func) should be used to derive the dotted path rather than the partial object's class.

These incorrect assumptions and missing relationships are encoded in ResolverMatch.__init__ (django/urls/resolvers.py).
StepsToReproduce: Create a view function, e.g. def my_view(request, a, b=None): ...
Create a partial of that view, e.g. partial_view = functools.partial(my_view, 'prefill', b='x')
Add a URL pattern whose callback is partial_view and capture additional args from the URL.
Resolve that URL via Django's resolver (e.g. resolve('/the/url/')).

Inspect the ResolverMatch returned (or print repr(result)). Observe that the printed func is 'functools.partial' and the prefilled values ('prefill', b='x') are not visible in the printed args/kwargs.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a functools.partial is used as the view callback, ResolverMatch.__repr__ should show the underlying function's dotted path (module + function/class name) and display the effective call arguments: positional arguments consisting of the partial's prefilled positional args followed by the URL-captured positional args, and keyword arguments consisting of the partial's keywords overridden by URL-captured kwargs.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: ResolverMatch.__repr__ prints the function as 'functools.partial' (the partial object's class) and only shows the URL-captured args/kwargs; any positional or keyword arguments provided when creating the functools.partial are not visible in the ResolverMatch representation.

What I learned (analysis of the code):
- AutoFieldMeta is defined as:

  @property
  def _subclasses(self):
      return (BigAutoField, SmallAutoField)

  def __instancecheck__(self, instance):
      return isinstance(instance, self._subclasses) or super().__instancecheck__(instance)

  def __subclasscheck__(self, subclass):
      return subclass in self._subclasses or super().__subclasscheck__(subclass)

- AutoField itself is declared using metaclass=AutoFieldMeta.
- BigAutoField and SmallAutoField are normal classes defined in the same file.

Root cause
- __instancecheck__ is implemented using isinstance(instance, self._subclasses). This is fine — isinstance(x, (BigAutoField,)) will return True for instances whose class is a subclass of BigAutoField.
- __subclasscheck__, however, uses "subclass in self._subclasses". That checks identity (is the provided class exactly BigAutoField or SmallAutoField), not subclass relationship. Therefore, a user-defined subclass of BigAutoField (e.g. class MyBigAutoField(BigAutoField): pass) will not be found by "subclass in self._subclasses", and so issubclass(MyBigAutoField, AutoField) (which triggers AutoFieldMeta.__subclasscheck__) will incorrectly return False (unless super().__subclasscheck__ handles it, but it won't since AutoField itself isn't in the MRO of MyBigAutoField).
- Because Options._get_default_pk_class() uses issubclass(pk_class, AutoField), a custom subclass will fail that check and raise the misleading ValueError: "must subclass AutoField."

Correct fix
- Change AutoFieldMeta.__subclasscheck__ to test subclassing properly (use issubclass(subclass, self._subclasses) rather than membership). Also be defensive in case non-class values are passed (TypeError from issubclass), falling back to the previous behavior or to super.

Exact code change
- File to change: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py
- Method to change: AutoFieldMeta.__subclasscheck__

Current code (excerpt):
  def __subclasscheck__(self, subclass):
      return subclass in self._subclasses or super().__subclasscheck__(subclass)

Suggested replacement (full method):

  def __subclasscheck__(self, subclass):
      """
      Recognize subclasses of the classes in _subclasses as AutoField subclasses.

      Previously this used 'subclass in self._subclasses' which only matched
      exact identity (e.g. BigAutoField), not subclasses thereof (e.g.
      user-defined MyBigAutoField(BigAutoField)).
      """
      try:
          # self._subclasses is a tuple of classes; issubclass supports a tuple,
          # returning True if `subclass` is a subclass of any element.
          return issubclass(subclass, self._subclasses) or super().__subclasscheck__(subclass)
      except TypeError:
          # `subclass` wasn't a class/type; fall back to the previous identity check
          # and to the default implementation.
          return subclass in self._subclasses or super().__subclasscheck__(subclass)

Why this fixes it
- issubclass(subclass, self._subclasses) returns True for any subclass of BigAutoField or SmallAutoField (including user-defined ones), so issubclass(MyBigAutoField, AutoField) will correctly be True via the metaclass logic.
- The try/except makes the logic robust if something that isn't a class is passed.

Other locations affected
- No other code paths need to be changed to make DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD accept user subclasses of BigAutoField / SmallAutoField. The instance-level check (__instancecheck__) already used isinstance(instance, self._subclasses) which already handles instances of subclasses, so it is fine.

bug_report.Title: DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD rejects user subclasses of BigAutoField/SmallAutoField (subclass check bug)
bug_report.Description: When DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD is set to a user-defined subclass of BigAutoField or SmallAutoField, Django raises a ValueError during model import claiming the class does not subclass AutoField.
bug_report.RootCause: 1) AutoFieldMeta.__subclasscheck__ in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py implements the subclass test using membership ("subclass in self._subclasses"), which checks identity (exact class equality) rather than subclass relationships. This makes a custom subclass (e.g. class MyBigAutoField(BigAutoField)) fail the check. 2) options._get_default_pk_class in django/db/models/options.py calls issubclass(pk_class, AutoField); because AutoFieldMeta.__subclasscheck__ returns False for user subclasses of BigAutoField/SmallAutoField, that issubclass(...) call incorrectly fails and triggers the ValueError: "Primary key '<path>' referred by DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD must subclass AutoField." 3) The instance-level check (AutoFieldMeta.__instancecheck__, which uses isinstance(instance, self._subclasses)) already handles instances of subclasses correctly; the defect is limited to the class/subclass check. 4) The correct relationship that should be tested (and that will recognize user subclasses) is: issubclass(subclass, self._subclasses) (or an equivalent that returns True when the provided class is a subclass of any class in self._subclasses).
StepsToReproduce: In settings, set DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD = "example.core.models.MyBigAutoField"
Run any manage.py command that imports apps (e.g., python manage.py check or python manage.py runserver).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Django accepts a DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD that names a user-defined subclass of BigAutoField or SmallAutoField. The named class is treated as a valid AutoField subclass and model import proceeds without raising a ValueError.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Django raises a ValueError during app/model import: "Primary key 'example.core/models.MyBigAutoField' referred by DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD must subclass AutoField." The traceback originates while importing models and during Options._get_default_pk_class() when issubclass(pk_class, AutoField) is evaluated.

class AdminScriptTestCase(SimpleTestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        tmpdir = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
        self.addCleanup(tmpdir.cleanup)
        # os.path.realpath() is required for temporary directories on macOS,
        # where `/var` is a symlink to `/private/var`.
        self.test_dir = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(tmpdir.name, 'test_project'))
        os.mkdir(self.test_dir)

    def write_settings(self, filename, apps=None, is_dir=False, sdict=None, extra=None):
        if is_dir:
            settings_dir = os.path.join(self.test_dir, filename)
            os.mkdir(settings_dir)
            settings_file_path = os.path.join(settings_dir, '__init__.py')
        else:
            settings_file_path = os.path.join(self.test_dir, filename)

        with open(settings_file_path, 'w') as settings_file:
            settings_file.write('# Settings file automatically generated by admin_scripts test case\n')
            if extra:
                settings_file.write("%s\n" % extra)
            exports = [
                'DATABASES',
                'DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD',
                'ROOT_URLCONF',
                'SECRET_KEY',
            ]
            for s in exports:
                if hasattr(settings, s):
                    o = getattr(settings, s)
                    if not isinstance(o, (dict, tuple, list)):
                        o = "'%s'" % o
                    settings_file.write("%s = %s\n" % (s, o))

            if apps is None:
                apps = ['django.contrib.auth', 'django.contrib.contenttypes', 'admin_scripts']

            settings_file.write("INSTALLED_APPS = %s\n" % apps)

            if sdict:
                for k, v in sdict.items():
                    settings_file.write("%s = %s\n" % (k, v))

    def _ext_backend_paths(self):
        """
        Returns the paths for any external backend packages.
        """
        paths = []
        for backend in settings.DATABASES.values():
            package = backend['ENGINE'].split('.')[0]
            if package != 'django':
                backend_pkg = __import__(package)
                backend_dir = os.path.dirname(backend_pkg.__file__)
                paths.append(os.path.dirname(backend_dir))
        return paths

    def run_test(self, args, settings_file=None, apps=None):
        base_dir = os.path.dirname(self.test_dir)
        # The base dir for Django's tests is one level up.
        tests_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(__file__))
        # The base dir for Django is one level above the test dir. We don't use
        # `import django` to figure that out, so we don't pick up a Django
        # from site-packages or similar.
        django_dir = os.path.dirname(tests_dir)
        ext_backend_base_dirs = self._ext_backend_paths()

        # Define a temporary environment for the subprocess
        test_environ = os.environ.copy()

        # Set the test environment
        if settings_file:
            test_environ['DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE'] = settings_file
        elif 'DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE' in test_environ:
            del test_environ['DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE']
        python_path = [base_dir, django_dir, tests_dir]
        python_path.extend(ext_backend_base_dirs)
        test_environ['PYTHONPATH'] = os.pathsep.join(python_path)
        test_environ['PYTHONWARNINGS'] = ''

        p = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, *args],
            stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
            cwd=self.test_dir,
            env=test_environ, universal_newlines=True,
        )
        return p.stdout, p.stderr

    def run_django_admin(self, args, settings_file=None):
        return self.run_test(['-m', 'django', *args], settings_file)

    def run_manage(self, args, settings_file=None, manage_py=None):
        template_manage_py = (
            os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), manage_py)
            if manage_py else
            os.path.join(os.path.dirname(conf.__file__), 'project_template', 'manage.py-tpl')
        )
        test_manage_py = os.path.join(self.test_dir, 'manage.py')
        shutil.copyfile(template_manage_py, test_manage_py)

        with open(test_manage_py) as fp:
            manage_py_contents = fp.read()
        manage_py_contents = manage_py_contents.replace(
            "{{ project_name }}", "test_project")
        with open(test_manage_py, 'w') as fp:
            fp.write(manage_py_contents)

        return self.run_test(['./manage.py', *args], settings_file)

    def assertNoOutput(self, stream):
        "Utility assertion: assert that the given stream is empty"
        self.assertEqual(len(stream), 0, "Stream should be empty: actually contains '%s'" % stream)

    def assertOutput(self, stream, msg, regex=False):
        "Utility assertion: assert that the given message exists in the output"
        if regex:
            self.assertIsNotNone(
                re.search(msg, stream),
                "'%s' does not match actual output text '%s'" % (msg, stream)
            )
        else:
            self.assertIn(msg, stream, "'%s' does not match actual output text '%s'" % (msg, stream))

    def assertNotInOutput(self, stream, msg):
        "Utility assertion: assert that the given message doesn't exist in the output"
        self.assertNotIn(msg, stream, "'%s' matches actual output text '%s'" % (msg, stream))

    def test_base_run_from_argv(self):
        """
        Test run_from_argv properly terminates even with custom execute() (#19665)
        Also test proper traceback display.
        """
        err = StringIO()
        command = BaseCommand(stderr=err)

        def raise_command_error(*args, **kwargs):
            raise CommandError("Custom error")

        command.execute = lambda args: args  # This will trigger TypeError

        # If the Exception is not CommandError it should always
        # raise the original exception.
        with self.assertRaises(TypeError):
            command.run_from_argv(['', ''])

        # If the Exception is CommandError and --traceback is not present
        # this command should raise a SystemExit and don't print any
        # traceback to the stderr.
        command.execute = raise_command_error
        err.truncate(0)
        with self.assertRaises(SystemExit):
            command.run_from_argv(['', ''])
        err_message = err.getvalue()
        self.assertNotIn("Traceback", err_message)
        self.assertIn("CommandError", err_message)

        # If the Exception is CommandError and --traceback is present
        # this command should raise the original CommandError as if it
        # were not a CommandError.
        err.truncate(0)
        with self.assertRaises(CommandError):
            command.run_from_argv(['', '', '--traceback'])

        UnicodeDecodeError in run_from_argv.

            raise CommandError("Erreur personnalisée")

        command = BaseCommand(stderr=StringIO())
        command.execute = raise_command_error

        with self.assertRaises(SystemExit):
            command.run_from_argv(['', ''])

    def test_run_from_argv_closes_connections(self):
        """

        being executed (#21255).
        """
        command = BaseCommand()
        command.check = lambda: []

class ArgumentOrder(AdminScriptTestCase):
    """Tests for 2-stage argument parsing scheme.

    django-admin command arguments are parsed in 2 parts; the core arguments
    (--settings, --traceback and --pythonpath) are parsed using a basic parser,
    ignoring any unknown options. Then the full settings are
    passed to the command parser, which extracts commands of interest to the
    individual command.
    """
    def setUp(self):
        super().setUp()
        self.write_settings('settings.py', apps=['django.contrib.auth', 'django.contrib.contenttypes'])
        self.write_settings('alternate_settings.py')

    def test_setting_then_option(self):
        """ Options passed after settings are correctly handled. """
        args = ['base_command', 'testlabel', '--settings=alternate_settings', '--option_a=x']
        self._test(args)

    def test_setting_then_short_option(self):
        """ Short options passed after settings are correctly handled. """
        args = ['base_command', 'testlabel', '--settings=alternate_settings', '-a', 'x']
        self._test(args)

    def test_option_then_setting(self):
        """ Options passed before settings are correctly handled. """
        args = ['base_command', 'testlabel', '--option_a=x', '--settings=alternate_settings']
        self._test(args)

    def test_short_option_then_setting(self):
        """ Short options passed before settings are correctly handled. """
        args = ['base_command', 'testlabel', '-a', 'x', '--settings=alternate_settings']
        self._test(args)

    def test_option_then_setting_then_option(self):
        """ Options are correctly handled when they are passed before and after
        a setting. """
        args = ['base_command', 'testlabel', '--option_a=x', '--settings=alternate_settings', '--option_b=y']
        self._test(args, option_b="'y'")

    def _test(self, args, option_b="'2'"):
        out, err = self.run_manage(args)
        self.assertNoOutput(err)
        self.assertOutput(
            out,
            "EXECUTE:BaseCommand labels=('testlabel',), options=["
            "('force_color', False), ('no_color', False), ('option_a', 'x'), "
            "('option_b', %s), ('option_c', '3'), ('pythonpath', None), "
            "('settings', 'alternate_settings'), ('traceback', False), "
            "('verbosity', 1)]" % option_b
        )

Thought: Summary of investigation
- I started from the bug report pointing at django/core/management/templates.py line ~77: self.validate_name(os.path.basename(target), 'directory').
- I inspected django/core/management/templates.py in full to see how target is used and validated.
- I searched for other usages of validate_name(os.path.basename(...)) and os.path.basename(...) across the codebase to find other potential occurrences; the only problematic call is the one in templates.py.
- I inspected the tests (tests/admin_scripts/tests.py) and found existing coverage for trailing slashes in startproject templates; there was no test covering passing a destination directory with a trailing slash to startapp. I located the StartApp test class where a regression test should be added.

Root cause
- On POSIX, os.path.basename('directory/') returns '' (an empty string). TemplateCommand.handle calls validate_name(os.path.basename(target), 'directory') before normalizing/expanding the target path. When a user passes a target path ending with a trailing slash (for example via shell tab-completion), basename(target) becomes an empty string and validate_name('') raises CommandError: '' is not a valid app directory.
- The code does not account for trailing separators before taking the basename.

Correct fix and rationale
- Normalize the target path (to remove trailing separators) before calling os.path.basename for validation.
- Use os.path.normpath(os.path.expanduser(target)) or simply os.path.normpath(target) before basename. Using os.path.normpath is preferable to target.rstrip(os.sep) because:
  - It removes redundant separators and up-level references in a platform-consistent way.
  - rstrip(os.sep) would remove platform-specific separator only; users could still pass the other separator style (e.g., '/' on Windows), so rstrip('/') or rstrip('\\') is fragile.
- So change:
    self.validate_name(os.path.basename(target), 'directory')
  to:
    self.validate_name(os.path.basename(os.path.normpath(target)), 'directory')
- This handles inputs like 'apps/', 'apps//' and also normalizes things like 'apps/.' etc. It preserves existing validation semantics in other corner cases (e.g. passing '/' or 'C:\\' still yields an empty basename and thereby remains invalid, as it should).

All places that need changes
1) django/core/management/templates.py
   - Current code (around lines 75-79):
       else:
           if app_or_project == 'app':
               self.validate_name(os.path.basename(target), 'directory')
           top_dir = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser(target))
           ...
   - Problem: basename(target) can be '' when target ends with a trailing separator.
   - Fix: normalize target before calling basename:
       else:
           if app_or_project == 'app':
               # Normalize to strip trailing separators (e.g. 'dir/' -> 'dir')
               dir_name = os.path.basename(os.path.normpath(target))
               self.validate_name(dir_name, 'directory')
           top_dir = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser(target))
           ...
   - Why this is enough: The normalization is only needed for extracting the last path component for name validation; the rest of the code still uses expanduser/abspath for the actual target path.

- I also added a test to prevent regressions and to cover the specific case (trailing separators appended by shell tab-completion).
- I considered and explained why os.path.normpath is better than rstrip(os.sep) (handles cross-platform input and both separator styles).

Patch (conceptual)

bug_report.Title: django-admin startapp fails when target directory ends with trailing slash
bug_report.Description: Running django-admin startapp with a destination directory that includes a trailing path separator (e.g. django-admin startapp name directory/) raises a CommandError instead of creating the app.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect assumption: TemplateCommand assumes os.path.basename(target) yields the intended app directory name. Location: django/core/management/templates.py (TemplateCommand.handle, around line ~77). Evidence: on POSIX, os.path.basename('directory/') returns '' (empty string), so validate_name(os.path.basename(target), 'directory') receives '' and raises CommandError.

2) Wrong ordering: name validation is performed on the raw target before normalizing/expanding the path. Location: same file, TemplateCommand.handle (validation occurs before top_dir = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser(target))). The later normalization does not prevent the earlier empty basename.

3) Scope of impact and tests: only one occurrence of validate_name(os.path.basename(...)) was found in the codebase (templates.py), and there is no existing test covering startapp when the destination ends with a trailing separator. Location: repository-wide search summarized by the investigation.

4) Correct relationship for validation: the last path component used for name validation must be extracted from a normalized path. Concretely, dirname_for_validation should be computed as os.path.basename(os.path.normpath(target)) (or equivalently normalize target before basename). Rationale preserved from investigation: os.path.normpath(target) strips redundant/trailing separators and handles up-level references in a platform-consistent way; using target.rstrip(os.sep) is fragile across separator styles.
StepsToReproduce: Create (or ensure existence of) a parent directory, e.g. mkdir apps
Run: django-admin startapp trailing apps/
Observe that the command raises an error and does not create apps/trailing
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: django-admin startapp should accept a destination directory specified with a trailing path separator (e.g. 'apps/') and create the new app directory (e.g. 'apps/trailing') without raising an error.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The command fails with: CommandError: '' is not a valid app directory. The new app directory is not created.

bug_report.Title: Admin label 'for' attribute points to non-labelable ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget element
bug_report.Description: In the admin user form, the generated <label> for the ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget contains a for="..." attribute that points to the widget's rendered element (a <div> with an id). The widget does not render a labelable control (input/select/textarea), so the label's for attribute is invalid.
bug_report.RootCause: 1. ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget (django/contrib/auth/forms.py) renders textual output (a div) and not a labelable form control, but it uses the default Widget.id_for_label behavior which returns the provided id. 2. BoundField.label_tag (django/forms/boundfield.py) calls widget.id_for_label(id_) and, if it returns a non-empty value, emits a for="..." attribute on the <label>. Because ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget.id_for_label currently returns the id (default), label_tag creates a for attribute that points to a non-labelable element. 3. The correct relationship: for a widget that does not render a labelable element, id_for_label must return None (or a falsey value). In this case, ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget.id_for_label should return None so BoundField.label_tag omits the for attribute. (Location: django/contrib/auth/forms.py — class ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget; affected behavior location: django/forms/boundfield.py — BoundField.label_tag.)
StepsToReproduce: Open the Django admin user change form (where the password field uses ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget).
Inspect the HTML for the password field's label and widget.
Observe that the <label> element has a for="id_password" attribute while the widget renders a <div id="id_password"> (no input/select/textarea).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The label for the password display should not contain a for attribute when the associated widget does not render a labelable form control; the label should be plain (no for) while the widget may still render an id on its element for styling/JS.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The label contains a for attribute (e.g. for="id_password") that points to a non-labelable element (a <div>), producing invalid/meaningless HTML linkage.

bug_report.Title: BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores per-option id set by ChoiceWidget.create_option
bug_report.Description: When rendering subwidgets for multi-option widgets (e.g. CheckboxSelectMultiple), BoundWidget.id_for_label constructs an id from the name and index and ignores any id present in the option's attrs. As a result, label 'for' attributes rendered from BoundWidget.id_for_label can differ from the actual input element id produced by ChoiceWidget.create_option, causing mismatched labels/inputs when auto_id is customized or the parent widget supplies an explicit id.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BoundWidget.id_for_label (django/forms/boundfield.py) unconditionally returns 'id_%(name)s_%(index)s' using self.data['name'] and self.data['index'], ignoring any explicit id already present in the option's attrs.

2) ChoiceWidget.create_option (django/forms/widgets.py) sets per-option ids in option_attrs by calling widget.id_for_label(option_attrs['id'], index) when the parent widget has an id or auto_id; that id is stored at self.data['attrs']['id'] in the option dict. Because BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores self.data['attrs']['id'], label for= attributes produced from BoundWidget mismatch the input element id created by ChoiceWidget.

3) The incorrect assumption encoded in django/forms/boundfield.py is: "the canonical id for a subwidget can always be reconstructed as 'id_<name>_<index>'", which is false when auto_id is a format string or when the parent widget provides a specific id. The correct relationship is: when an option dict contains a generated id in option_attrs['id'], BoundWidget.id_for_label must return that id; otherwise fallback to the legacy 'id_<name>_<index>' construction (or empty string if name/index are missing).
StepsToReproduce: Create a form field with a ChoiceWidget-based multi-option widget (e.g. CheckboxSelectMultiple) and set a custom auto_id or attrs={'id': 'custom'} on the widget.
Render the field's subwidgets (e.g. iterate bound_field.subwidgets() or use the BoundWidget instances in templates).

Observe that each option's input element has an id attribute (e.g. 'custom_0', created by ChoiceWidget.create_option), but the label rendered using BoundWidget.id_for_label has a different id (e.g. 'id_<name>_0').
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: For multi-option widgets, each subwidget's label 'for' attribute should match the actual input element id generated for that option (i.e. the per-option id stored in the option dict's attrs['id'] when present). If no per-option id is present, label rendering should fall back to the appropriate legacy behavior (no 'for' attribute or a consistent constructed id).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: BoundWidget.id_for_label always returns a constructed id of the form 'id_<name>_<index>' and ignores self.data['attrs']['id'], causing the label 'for' attribute to point to a different id than the input element when the parent widget provided a custom id or auto_id format.

Investigation plan / reasoning
- The bug report describes migrations generated with a bases tuple containing a custom app model/mixin (imported as import app.models) and models.Model, but the generated migration is missing the import for django.db.models (so models is undefined).
- The migration writer/serializer code is responsible for producing serialized Python text and import lines. The likely culprits are:
  - django.db.migrations.serializer (builds string/inports for serialized values)
  - django.db.migrations.writer (collects imports and renders header)
- I will inspect MigrationWriter and the migration serializer to see how types (like models.Model) are serialized and which imports they request.

What I examined
1) django/db/migrations/writer.py
- This file gathers imports reported by serializers, then:
  - If "from django.db import models" is present in imports, it merges it into "from django.db import migrations, models".
  - Otherwise it ensures at least "from django.db import migrations" is present.
- Thus, serializers must return "from django.db import models" when they produce "models.X" strings in order for the writer to include the models import.

2) django/db/migrations/serializer.py
- This file contains TypeSerializer which handles serializing type objects (classes) to strings and returning required imports.
- The special_cases in TypeSerializer currently contain:
    (models.Model, "models.Model", [])
  i.e. models.Model is serialized as "models.Model" but returns an empty imports list.
- This is the root problem: TypeSerializer emits the literal "models.Model" but does not return the import "from django.db import models", so the MigrationWriter never sees that import and thus doesn't include it in the generated migration file. That produces a migration referencing models.Model without models being defined.

Reproduction reasoning
- In the report, bases were produced as (app.models.MyMixin, models.Model).
  - app.models.MyMixin gets serialized via DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path or FunctionTypeSerializer as "app.models.MyMixin" with import "import app.models".
  - models.Model gets serialized as "models.Model" without declaring "from django.db import models".
- MigrationWriter collects imports: e.g. {"import app.models", "from django.db import migrations"} (but no models import).
- The generated migration has "import app.models" and "from django.db import migrations", but not "from django.db import models". Hence NameError: models is undefined.

Root cause
- TypeSerializer special-cases models.Model by returning the string "models.Model" but returns no import. It must also request the "from django.db import models" import so that MigrationWriter adds the models import line to the migration file (and merges it with migrations import where appropriate).

Complete fix
- Change TypeSerializer.special_cases entry for models.Model to return imports including "from django.db import models" instead of an empty list.

Files/locations to change
1) django/db/migrations/serializer.py
- Current relevant code (excerpt):
  class TypeSerializer(BaseSerializer):
      def serialize(self):
          special_cases = [
              (models.Model, "models.Model", []),

          for case, string, imports in special_cases:
              if case is self.value:
                  return string, set(imports)
          ...

  class TypeSerializer(BaseSerializer):
      def serialize(self):
          special_cases = [
              (models.Model, "models.Model", ["from django.db import models"]),
              (type(None), 'type(None)', []),
          ]
          for case, string, imports in special_cases:
              if case is self.value:
                  return string, set(imports)
          ...

- Rationale: now serializing models.Model will both render "models.Model" and request the import "from django.db import models"; MigrationWriter will merge that with the migrations import as it already does (resulting in "from django.db import migrations, models") when the migrations import exists, or otherwise include "from django.db import models" as needed.

bug_report.Title: makemigrations output omits 'from django.db import models' when serializing models.Model in bases
bug_report.Description: When makemigrations serializes a model whose bases include a user-defined class from app.models and django.db.models.Model, the generated migration references models.Model but does not include the required import for django.db.models, causing NameError: name 'models' is not defined when importing the migration.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/migrations/serializer.py : TypeSerializer special-case for django.db.models.Model encodes the assumption that serializing models.Model does not require any import. The code currently returns the string "models.Model" with an empty imports set ([]). This is incorrect because the writer requires the explicit import string "from django.db import models" to render models in the migration header. The correct relationship is: for models.Model the serializer must return imports containing exactly "from django.db import models" (i.e. special_cases entry should supply ["from django.db import models"]).

2) django/db/migrations/writer.py : MigrationWriter relies on serializers to report the exact import string "from django.db import models" in order to merge it into the migration file header (it transforms presence of that string into "from django.db import migrations, models"). The writer's merging logic therefore depends on serializers returning that explicit import string; since TypeSerializer omits it, the writer never inserts the models import. This is a required string-level contract between serializers and the writer.

3) tests/migrations/test_writer.py : There is no regression test asserting that serializing a tuple of (user module class, models.Model) yields imports that include "from django.db import models". The missing test coverage allowed the incorrect serializer behavior to go undetected.
StepsToReproduce: Create app/models.py with the following contents:
from django.db import models
class MyField(models.TextField):
pass
class MyBaseModel(models.Model):
class Meta:
abstract = True
class MyMixin:
pass
class MyModel(MyMixin, MyBaseModel):
name = MyField(primary_key=True)
Run: python manage.py makemigrations
Inspect the generated migration file (app/migrations/0001_initial.py) and observe the bases tuple contains models.Model but there is no 'from django.db import models' import.
Attempt to run/manage the migration; importing the migration raises NameError: name 'models' is not defined.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: makemigrations generates a valid Python migration file. If a generated migration references models.Model (as e.g. bases=(app.models.MyMixin, models.Model)), the file includes the corresponding import statement so 'models' is defined (for example via 'from django.db import models' or the combined 'from django.db import migrations, models').
