bug_report.Title: template filter `join` escapes separator even when `{% autoescape off %}` is used
bug_report.Description: The template filter `join` escapes the joining string (separator) even when template autoescaping is disabled via `{% autoescape off %}`, causing HTML in the separator variable to be HTML-escaped in the rendered output.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/template/defaultfilters.py, function join(value, arg, autoescape=True): the implementation unconditionally calls conditional_escape(arg).join(value), i.e. it always applies conditional_escape to the separator argument regardless of the autoescape flag. This encodes the incorrect assumption that the separator must always be escaped. (Current formula: data = conditional_escape(arg).join(value) — applied regardless of autoescape.)

2) Correct relationship / intended behavior (preserve in implementation/tests): the separator should only be escaped when autoescape is True. The correct logic is: if autoescape is True then
   - value = [conditional_escape(v) for v in value]
   - sep = conditional_escape(arg)
   else
   - sep = arg
   data = sep.join(value)
   (i.e. only apply conditional_escape to arg and elements when autoescape is True). This relationship is absent from the current implementation and must be encoded at the same location (django/template/defaultfilters.py, join).

3) tests/template_tests/filter_tests/test_join.py (FunctionTests.test_autoescape_off) encodes the old, incorrect expectation (that the separator is escaped even when autoescape=False). The regression test added in tests/template_tests/filter_tests/test_regression.py (join02) demonstrates the template-level failure; the unit test named above presently enforces the wrong behavior and should be updated to expect an unescaped separator when autoescape is False.
StepsToReproduce: Create a template that disables autoescaping and uses the join filter with a variable separator, for example: '{% autoescape off %}{{ some_list|join:some_var }}{% endautoescape %}'.

Render the template with context: some_list = ['

Hello World!

', 'beta & me', ''] and some_var = '
'
Observe the rendered output.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When template autoescaping is disabled (via '{% autoescape off %}') the rendered output should include the separator variable verbatim (not HTML-escaped). When autoescaping is enabled, both list items and the separator should be escaped as appropriate.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior:
With autoescape off, the separator variable is HTML-escaped in the rendered result. Example observed output from the failing test: '

Hello World!

<br/>beta & me<br/>' (expected: '

Hello World!


beta & me
').

    def get_default_columns(
        self, select_mask, start_alias=None, opts=None, from_parent=None
    ):

        model. Will sometimes be called to pull in related models (e.g. via
        select_related), in which case "opts" and "start_alias" will be given
        to provide a starting point for the traversal.

        Return a list of strings, quoted appropriately for use in SQL
        directly, as well as a set of aliases used in the select statement (if
        'as_pairs' is True, return a list of (alias, col_name) pairs instead
        of strings as the first component and None as the second component).
        """

        if opts is None:
            if (opts := self.query.get_meta()) is None:
                return result

        # The 'seen_models' is used to optimize checking the needed parent
        # alias for a given field. This also includes None -> start_alias to
        # be used by local fields.
        seen_models = {None: start_alias}

        for field in opts.concrete_fields:
            model = field.model._meta.concrete_model

            # will assign None if the field belongs to this model.
            if model == opts.model:
                model = None

                from_parent

                and issubclass(
                    from_parent._meta.concrete_model, model._meta.concrete_model
                )

                # We end up here in the case select_related() resolution
                # proceeds from parent model to child model. In that case the
                # parent model data is already present in the SELECT clause,
                # and we want to avoid reloading the same data again.
                continue

                continue
            alias = self.query.join_parent_model(opts, model, start_alias, seen_models)
            column = field.get_col(alias)

Thought: Step 1 — classify the report (what I looked for)
- I extracted the main entities from the report: QuerySet.only(), select_related(), reverse OneToOneField relation.
- That indicated the bug is in how the SQL selection mask (only()/defer related logic) interacts with select_related's handling of reverse relations.

Step 2 — files/methods to inspect (and why)
- I opened django/db/models/query.py to find QuerySet.only(), which calls Query.add_immediate_loading(), so the real work is in the SQL Query representation.
- I opened django/db/models/sql/query.py to inspect the logic that turns deferred/immediate loading masks into a select_mask (methods _get_defer_select_mask, _get_only_select_mask, get_select_mask).
- I opened django/db/models/sql/compiler.py to see how select_mask is consumed when building the SELECT list (get_select/get_related_selections/get_default_columns).

What I learned from reading the code
- QuerySet.only(...) ends up calling Query.add_immediate_loading(fields) which sets Query.deferred_loading (a mask).
- Query.get_select_mask() converts Query.deferred_loading into a nested dictionary "select_mask" via either _get_defer_select_mask (when deferring) or _get_only_select_mask (when "only" is used).
- The SQLCompiler uses that select_mask to decide which columns to include in the SELECT (get_default_columns + get_related_selections).
- get_related_selections expects keys in select_mask for forward and reverse relations to be Field objects (for forward: key is the forward Field; for reverse: key is still the forward Field on the related model — see how it looks up select_mask.get(related_field) where related_field is a Field object).
- _get_defer_select_mask handles reverse relations specially: when a mask entry corresponds to a reverse (or filtered) relation, it resolves to the underlying forward Field and stores the nested mask under that Field (or for filtered relations it uses the (name, relation) tuple key).
- However _get_only_select_mask (used for "only()" semantics) is implemented incorrectly: it unconditionally does field = opts.get_field(field_name) then select_mask.setdefault(field, {}), which for reverse relation names yields a ForeignObjectRel object (reverse relation object), not the underlying forward Field. That leads to keys in select_mask that do not match what get_related_selections expects (which looks up by the forward Field). As a result, related select masking is ignored and all fields from the related model are included in the SQL.
- This precisely matches the bug report: reverse OneToOne relation used via select_related('secondary') together with only('secondary__secondary_field_1') results in the related model's fields all being included (select_mask lookup fails), whereas earlier Django handled it correctly.

Root cause
- _get_only_select_mask does not treat reverse relation lookups the same way as _get_defer_select_mask: it stores the nested mask under the ForeignObjectRel (reverse relation object) rather than under the forward Field of the relation. Therefore get_related_selections cannot find the mask for reverse related models and falls back to selecting all columns.

Complete fix (what to change)
- Update Query._get_only_select_mask in django/db/models/sql/query.py to mirror the logic used in _get_defer_select_mask for resolving reverse and filtered relations. Concretely:
  - If the mask key corresponds to a filtered relation name (present in self._filtered_relations), set the nested select mask under the key (field_name, relation) like _get_defer_select_mask does, and use the underlying relation.field for recursion.
  - Else, handle the case where opts.get_field(field_name) returns a reverse relation (ForeignObjectRel / related object): if it has attribute .field, use that underlying Field and set the select_mask key to the Field (not to the ForeignObjectRel).
  - Otherwise treat it as a normal Field and use it as key, just like the current code for forward relations.
  - Recurse using self._get_only_select_mask for nested masks.

- No other locations in the codebase need changing: the bug is entirely in the _get_only_select_mask implementation. The rest of the code (compiler.get_related_selections and _get_defer_select_mask) already expects/uses the Field keys and filtered-relation tuple keys; _get_only_select_mask must produce the same key shapes.

Patch (conceptual diff)
Replace current implementation of _get_only_select_mask (in django/db/models/sql/query.py) with code that mirrors the reverse-handling in _get_defer_select_mask.

Here is the corrected function body (apply in django/db/models/sql/query.py):

            select_mask = {}
        select_mask[opts.pk] = {}
        # Only include fields mentioned in the mask.

Fixed implementation:
    def _get_only_select_mask(self, opts, mask, select_mask=None):
        if select_mask is None:
            select_mask = {}
        select_mask[opts.pk] = {}
        # Only include fields mentioned in the mask.
        for field_name, field_mask in mask.items():
            # Handle filtered relations and reverse relations the same way
            # _get_defer_select_mask does, so that select_mask keys match what
            # get_related_selections expects.
            if filtered_relation := self._filtered_relations.get(field_name):
                relation = opts.get_field(filtered_relation.relation_name)
                # Use the (name, relation) tuple key for filtered relations.
                field_select_mask = select_mask.setdefault((field_name, relation), {})
                field = relation.field
            else:
                reverse_rel = opts.get_field(field_name)
                # If this is a reverse relation object (ForeignObjectRel etc.)
                # use the underlying field (reverse_rel.field). Otherwise it's a
                # normal Field and can be used as-is.
                if hasattr(reverse_rel, "field"):
                    field = reverse_rel.field
                    field_select_mask = select_mask.setdefault(field, {})
                else:
                    field = reverse_rel
                    field_select_mask = select_mask.setdefault(field, {})
            if field_mask:
                if not field.is_relation:
                    raise FieldError(next(iter(field_mask)))
                related_model = field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model
                self._get_only_select_mask(related_model._meta, field_mask, field_select_mask)
        return select_mask

Notes / rationale
- This change makes _get_only_select_mask produce the same shape of select_mask as _get_defer_select_mask (and as get_related_selections expects), so that "only()" bitmasks are applied to reverse relations when select_related is used.
- This is a targeted, minimal change: only modifies _get_only_select_mask. No changes required in get_related_selections or in the compiler. They already implement correct lookups and support the filtered-relation (name, relation) tuple keys.

bug_report.Title: QuerySet.only() ignores field mask for select_related() on reverse OneToOneField (Django 4.2)
bug_report.Description: When using QuerySet.only(...) together with select_related(...) on a reverse OneToOneField relation, the SQL generated on Django 4.2 includes all columns from the related model instead of limiting the related-model columns to those named in only(). This regression is visible when running the sample query Main.objects.select_related('secondary').only('main_field_1', 'secondary__secondary_field_1').
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Query._get_only_select_mask (django/db/models/sql/query.py) constructs select_mask entries for reverse relation names using the reverse relation object (ForeignObjectRel) returned by opts.get_field(field_name) instead of the underlying forward Field object. get_related_selections and the SQL compiler expect select_mask keys to be the forward Field objects (i.e. the Field instance on the model that defines the relation). Because the key types differ, the related-model mask lookup fails and the compiler falls back to selecting all related columns.

2) Query._get_only_select_mask does not mirror the filtered-relation handling used by Query._get_defer_select_mask: for filtered relations _get_defer_select_mask stores nested masks under the (name, relation) tuple key and recurses using relation.field (the underlying forward Field). _get_only_select_mask does not produce the same key shape ((name, relation) tuple) nor use the underlying relation.field for recursion, so masked entries for filtered/reverse relations are not found by downstream code.

3) The higher-level interaction: QuerySet.only() uses Query.add_immediate_loading() to set Query.deferred_loading, which is converted into a nested select_mask by Query._get_only_select_mask. Because _get_only_select_mask produces keys that don't match the shapes consumed by the SQL compiler (get_related_selections/get_default_columns), the only() mask is ignored for reverse relations. (Relevant locations: django/db/models/query.py: Query.add_immediate_loading, django/db/models/sql/query.py: Query._get_only_select_mask and Query._get_defer_select_mask, and the SQL compiler's related-selection code that expects Field or (name, relation) tuple keys.)

Correct relationship required (evidence from investigation): select_mask keys must be either: (a) the forward Field object for the relation (so get_related_selections can do select_mask.get(related_field)), or (b) for filtered relations, the tuple (field_name, relation) as produced by _get_defer_select_mask. _get_only_select_mask must produce the same key shapes and recurse using the relation.field where appropriate.

    secondary_field_1 = models.CharField(blank=True, max_length=45)
    secondary_field_2 = models.CharField(blank=True, max_length=45)
    secondary_field_3 = models.CharField(blank=True, max_length=45)

Inspect the generated SQL (e.g. str(qs.query) or qs.query.sql_with_params()) and observe the SELECT clause for the related table.

from django.core.exceptions import FieldError
from django.db.models.sql.constants import CURSOR, GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE, NO_RESULTS
from django.db.models.sql.query import Query

__all__ = ["DeleteQuery", "UpdateQuery", "InsertQuery", "AggregateQuery"]


class DeleteQuery(Query):
    """A DELETE SQL query."""

    compiler = "SQLDeleteCompiler"

    def do_query(self, table, where, using):
        self.alias_map = {table: self.alias_map[table]}
        self.where = where
        cursor = self.get_compiler(using).execute_sql(CURSOR)
        if cursor:
            with cursor:
                return cursor.rowcount
        return 0

    def delete_batch(self, pk_list, using):
        """
        Set up and execute delete queries for all the objects in pk_list.

        More than one physical query may be executed if there are a
        lot of values in pk_list.
        """
        # number of objects deleted
        num_deleted = 0
        field = self.get_meta().pk
        for offset in range(0, len(pk_list), GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE):
            self.clear_where()
            self.add_filter(
                f"{field.attname}__in",
                pk_list[offset : offset + GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE],
            )
            num_deleted += self.do_query(
                self.get_meta().db_table, self.where, using=using
            )
        return num_deleted


class UpdateQuery(Query):
    """An UPDATE SQL query."""

    compiler = "SQLUpdateCompiler"

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._setup_query()

    def _setup_query(self):
        """
        Run on initialization and at the end of chaining. Any attributes that
        would normally be set in __init__() should go here instead.
        """
        self.values = []
        self.related_ids = None
        self.related_updates = {}

    def clone(self):
        obj = super().clone()
        obj.related_updates = self.related_updates.copy()
        return obj

    def update_batch(self, pk_list, values, using):
        self.add_update_values(values)
        for offset in range(0, len(pk_list), GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE):
            self.clear_where()
            self.add_filter(
                "pk__in", pk_list[offset : offset + GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE]
            )
            self.get_compiler(using).execute_sql(NO_RESULTS)

    def add_update_values(self, values):
        """
        Convert a dictionary of field name to value mappings into an update
        query. This is the entry point for the public update() method on
        querysets.
        """
        values_seq = []
        for name, val in values.items():
            field = self.get_meta().get_field(name)
            direct = (
                not (field.auto_created and not field.concrete) or not field.concrete
            )
            model = field.model._meta.concrete_model
            if not direct or (field.is_relation and field.many_to_many):
                raise FieldError(
                    "Cannot update model field %r (only non-relations and "
                    "foreign keys permitted)." % field
                )
            if model is not self.get_meta().concrete_model:
                self.add_related_update(model, field, val)
                continue
            values_seq.append((field, model, val))
        return self.add_update_fields(values_seq)

    def add_update_fields(self, values_seq):
        """
        Append a sequence of (field, model, value) triples to the internal list
        that will be used to generate the UPDATE query. Might be more usefully
        called add_update_targets() to hint at the extra information here.
        """
        for field, model, val in values_seq:
            if hasattr(val, "resolve_expression"):
                # Resolve expressions here so that annotations are no longer needed
                val = val.resolve_expression(self, allow_joins=False, for_save=True)
            self.values.append((field, model, val))

    def add_related_update(self, model, field, value):
        """
        Add (name, value) to an update query for an ancestor model.

        Update are coalesced so that only one update query per ancestor is run.
        """
        self.related_updates.setdefault(model, []).append((field, None, value))

    def get_related_updates(self):
        """
        Return a list of query objects: one for each update required to an
        ancestor model. Each query will have the same filtering conditions as
        the current query but will only update a single table.
        """
        if not self.related_updates:
            return []
        result = []
        for model, values in self.related_updates.items():
            query = UpdateQuery(model)
            query.values = values
            if self.related_ids is not None:
                query.add_filter("pk__in", self.related_ids[model])
            result.append(query)
        return result

- However the SQL generation supports RETURNING together with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (SQLInsertCompiler builds on_conflict suffix and will append RETURNING via return_insert_columns).   - The batch contains exactly 1 row and the backend supports returning columns from insert (connection.features.can_return_columns_from_insert) — single-row returns.
- Only allow this when on_conflict is None OR on_conflict == OnConflict.UPDATE (i.e., allow returning for update_conflicts), but keep ignore_conflicts behavior unchanged (do not request returning in ignore_conflicts).
  - Rationale for not changing ignore_conflicts: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING may return rows only for rows that were actually inserted; rows that were skipped produce no row. Mapping returned rows back to the input objects would be ambiguous for multi-row inserts, so keeping the prior behavior is conservative and consistent with the existing docs/behavior.

- Implementation details:
  - Compute want_returning per-batch item depending on connection features, batch size (len(item)), and on_conflict value.
  - Call _insert(...) with returning_fields=self.model._meta.db_returning_fields when want_returning is True. Always pass on_conflict, update_fields, unique_fields so the compiler constructs ON CONFLICT suffix correctly.

Exact code change (patch for django/db/models/query.py)

Proposed code (conceptual patch snippet — exact context in file is shown below):

In django/db/models/query.py, replace the loop in _batched_insert with:

    def _batched_insert(
        self,
        objs,
        fields,
        batch_size,
        on_conflict=None,
        update_fields=None,
        unique_fields=None,
    ):
        """
        Helper method for bulk_create() to insert objs one batch at a time.
        """
        connection = connections[self.db]
        ops = connection.ops
        max_batch_size = max(ops.bulk_batch_size(fields, objs), 1)
        batch_size = min(batch_size, max_batch_size) if batch_size else max_batch_size
        inserted_rows = []
        bulk_return = connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert
        can_return_columns = connection.features.can_return_columns_from_insert
        returning_fields = self.model._meta.db_returning_fields

        for item in [objs[i : i + batch_size] for i in range(0, len(objs), batch_size)]:
            # Decide whether we can/should request RETURNING for this batch.
            want_returning = False
            # Allow RETURNING for normal inserts when the backend can return rows
            if on_conflict is None:
                if bulk_return:
                    want_returning = True
            # Allow RETURNING for upserts (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE) when backend supports it:
            elif on_conflict == OnConflict.UPDATE:
                # Multi-row returning supported
                if bulk_return:
                    want_returning = True
                # If only a single row in this batch and backend supports returning columns
                elif len(item) == 1 and can_return_columns:
                    want_returning = True
            # For ignore_conflicts (OnConflict.IGNORE) we do not request RETURNING
            # because some backends (or semantics) may not return rows for ignored rows.

            if want_returning and returning_fields:
                rows = self._insert(
                    item,
                    fields=fields,
                    using=self.db,
                    on_conflict=on_conflict,
                    update_fields=update_fields,
                    unique_fields=unique_fields,
                    returning_fields=returning_fields,
                )
                # _insert returns rows only when returning_fields is provided.
                inserted_rows.extend(rows)
            else:
                # No RETURNING requested; just execute the insert/upsert.
                self._insert(
                    item,
                    fields=fields,
                    using=self.db,
                    on_conflict=on_conflict,
                    update_fields=update_fields,
                    unique_fields=unique_fields,
                )

        return inserted_rows

Notes on why this is safe
- SQLInsertCompiler supports placing the ON CONFLICT suffix and adding RETURNING clause afterwards. The PostgreSQL backend returns rows for RETURNING in upserts as expected (operations.return_insert_columns and fetch_returned_insert_rows show this).
- SQLInsertCompiler.execute_sql has an assertion that only permits returning fields when (len(objs) == 1) or connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert is True — our logic respects that: for multi-row batches we require bulk_return True; for single-row batches we allow returning if can_return_columns is True.
- We still avoid returning for ignore_conflicts to avoid ambiguities mapping returned rows to objects (consistent with current behavior).

bug_report.Title: bulk_create does not return primary keys when update_conflicts=True (upsert)
bug_report.Description: When QuerySet.bulk_create() is called with update_conflicts=True (upsert), the generated INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE query does not include a RETURNING clause and the created/updated instances do not get their primary key (and other db_returning_fields) populated, even though the database (PostgreSQL) accepts RETURNING with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and would return IDs.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect conditional logic in QuerySet._batched_insert (django/db/models/query.py): the code only passes model._meta.db_returning_fields to the low-level insert when on_conflict is None AND connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert is True. That encodes the assumption "do not request RETURNING for any ON CONFLICT path (both IGNORE and UPDATE)". This assumption is false for the UPDATE case because the SQLInsertCompiler and PostgreSQL support RETURNING together with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.

2) The correct relationship that should be used to decide whether to request returning_fields is:
   - Provide returning_fields when either:
     a) on_conflict is None AND connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert is True (existing allowed case), OR
     b) on_conflict == OnConflict.UPDATE AND (connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert is True OR (len(batch) == 1 AND connection.features.can_return_columns_from_insert is True)).
   This preserves the compiler.execute_sql requirement that returning_fields on multi-row inserts is only allowed if connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert is True, while allowing single-row returns when the backend supports returning columns from a single INSERT.

3) Supporting evidence / related locations:
   - SQLInsertCompiler assembles ON CONFLICT and RETURNING independently (django/db/models/sql/compiler.py). The compiler will append RETURNING when returning_fields is provided.
   - SQLInsertCompiler.execute_sql enforces that returning_fields are allowed only when len(objs) == 1 or connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert is True; the conditional in (2) above respects that assertion.
   - PostgreSQL backend operations generate RETURNING clauses and fetch the returned rows (django/db/backends/postgresql/operations.py), and manually appending RETURNING id to an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE returns the id in PostgreSQL (as observed by the reporter).

4) Intentional/undetermined design: ignoring returning_fields for ignore_conflicts (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) appears to be a conservative choice because DO NOTHING may return rows only for inserted rows (skipping conflicted rows), which makes mapping returned rows back to input objects ambiguous for multi-row inserts. The current code treats IGNORE the same as UPDATE, which is the part that is incorrect for UPDATE but defensible for IGNORE.
StepsToReproduce: Using PostgreSQL, define a model MyModel with an auto-increment primary key.
Create a list with one or more MyModel instances without setting pk.
Call MyModel.objects.bulk_create(objs, update_conflicts=True, update_fields=[...], unique_fields=[...])
Observe the generated SQL: it contains INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(...) DO UPDATE ... but no RETURNING my_model.id clause.
Note that after bulk_create completes, the instances in objs do not have their primary key attributes populated.
(Verification) Manually append RETURNING my_model.id to the generated SQL and run it in PostgreSQL; the id is returned by the database.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When calling bulk_create(..., update_conflicts=True) on a database backend that supports RETURNING for the requested operation, the database RETURNING columns (including the primary key) are returned and the corresponding attributes (primary key and any db_returning_fields) are populated on the instances passed to bulk_create. For multi-row inserts this requires the backend feature can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert; for single-row inserts this requires can_return_columns_from_insert.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: bulk_create(..., update_conflicts=True) executes INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE without a RETURNING clause. As a result, returned IDs are not available and the instances passed to bulk_create do not get their primary key (or other db_returning_fields) populated, even on PostgreSQL where RETURNING with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is supported.

import functools
import re
from collections import defaultdict
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter
from itertools import chain

from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models
from django.db.migrations import operations
from django.db.migrations.migration import Migration
from django.db.migrations.operations.models import AlterModelOptions
from django.db.migrations.optimizer import MigrationOptimizer
from django.db.migrations.questioner import MigrationQuestioner
from django.db.migrations.utils import (
    COMPILED_REGEX_TYPE,
    RegexObject,
    resolve_relation,
)


class MigrationAutodetector:
    """
    Take a pair of ProjectStates and compare them to see what the first would
    need doing to make it match the second (the second usually being the
    project's current state).

    Note that this naturally operates on entire projects at a time,
    as it's likely that changes interact (for example, you can't
    add a ForeignKey without having a migration to add the table it
    depends on first). A user interface may offer single-app usage
    if it wishes, with the caveat that it may not always be possible.
    """

    def __init__(self, from_state, to_state, questioner=None):
        self.from_state = from_state
        self.to_state = to_state
        self.questioner = questioner or MigrationQuestioner()
        self.existing_apps = {app for app, model in from_state.models}

    def changes(self, graph, trim_to_apps=None, convert_apps=None, migration_name=None):
        """
        Main entry point to produce a list of applicable changes.
        Take a graph to base names on and an optional set of apps
        to try and restrict to (restriction is not guaranteed)
        """
        changes = self._detect_changes(convert_apps, graph)
        changes = self.arrange_for_graph(changes, graph, migration_name)
        if trim_to_apps:
            changes = self._trim_to_apps(changes, trim_to_apps)
        return changes

    def deep_deconstruct(self, obj):
        """
        Recursive deconstruction for a field and its arguments.
        Used for full comparison for rename/alter; sometimes a single-level
        deconstruction will not compare correctly.
        """
        if isinstance(obj, list):
            return [self.deep_deconstruct(value) for value in obj]
        elif isinstance(obj, tuple):
            return tuple(self.deep_deconstruct(value) for value in obj)
        elif isinstance(obj, dict):
            return {key: self.deep_deconstruct(value) for key, value in obj.items()}
        elif isinstance(obj, functools.partial):
            return (
                obj.func,
                self.deep_deconstruct(obj.args),
                self.deep_deconstruct(obj.keywords),
            )
        elif isinstance(obj, COMPILED_REGEX_TYPE):
            return RegexObject(obj)
        elif isinstance(obj, type):
            # If this is a type that implements 'deconstruct' as an instance method,
            # avoid treating this as being deconstructible itself - see #22951
            return obj
        elif hasattr(obj, "deconstruct"):
            deconstructed = obj.deconstruct()
            if isinstance(obj, models.Field):
                # we have a field which also returns a name
                deconstructed = deconstructed[1:]
            path, args, kwargs = deconstructed
            return (
                path,
                [self.deep_deconstruct(value) for value in args],
                {key: self.deep_deconstruct(value) for key, value in kwargs.items()},
            )
        else:
            return obj

    def only_relation_agnostic_fields(self, fields):
        """
        Return a definition of the fields that ignores field names and
        what related fields actually relate to. Used for detecting renames (as
        the related fields change during renames).
        """
        fields_def = []
        for name, field in sorted(fields.items()):
            deconstruction = self.deep_deconstruct(field)
            if field.remote_field and field.remote_field.model:
                deconstruction[2].pop("to", None)
            fields_def.append(deconstruction)
        return fields_def

    def _detect_changes(self, convert_apps=None, graph=None):
        """
        Return a dict of migration plans which will achieve the
        change from from_state to to_state. The dict has app labels
        as keys and a list of migrations as values.

        The resulting migrations aren't specially named, but the names
        do matter for dependencies inside the set.

        convert_apps is the list of apps to convert to use migrations
        (i.e. to make initial migrations for, in the usual case)

        graph is an optional argument that, if provided, can help improve
        dependency generation and avoid potential circular dependencies.
        """
        # The first phase is generating all the operations for each app
        # and gathering them into a big per-app list.
        # Then go through that list, order it, and split into migrations to
        # resolve dependencies caused by M2Ms and FKs.
        self.generated_operations = {}
        self.altered_indexes = {}
        self.altered_constraints = {}
        self.renamed_fields = {}

        # Prepare some old/new state and model lists, separating
        # proxy models and ignoring unmigrated apps.
        self.old_model_keys = set()
        self.old_proxy_keys = set()
        self.old_unmanaged_keys = set()
        self.new_model_keys = set()
        self.new_proxy_keys = set()
        self.new_unmanaged_keys = set()
        for (app_label, model_name), model_state in self.from_state.models.items():
            if not model_state.options.get("managed", True):
                self.old_unmanaged_keys.add((app_label, model_name))
            elif app_label not in self.from_state.real_apps:
                if model_state.options.get("proxy"):
                    self.old_proxy_keys.add((app_label, model_name))
                else:
                    self.old_model_keys.add((app_label, model_name))

        for (app_label, model_name), model_state in self.to_state.models.items():
            if not model_state.options.get("managed", True):
                self.new_unmanaged_keys.add((app_label, model_name))
            elif app_label not in self.from_state.real_apps or (
                convert_apps and app_label in convert_apps
            ):
                if model_state.options.get("proxy"):
                    self.new_proxy_keys.add((app_label, model_name))
                else:
                    self.new_model_keys.add((app_label, model_name))

        self.from_state.resolve_fields_and_relations()
        self.to_state.resolve_fields_and_relations()

        # Renames have to come first
        self.generate_renamed_models()

        # Prepare lists of fields and generate through model map
        self._prepare_field_lists()
        self._generate_through_model_map()

        # Generate non-rename model operations
        self.generate_deleted_models()
        self.generate_created_models()
        self.generate_deleted_proxies()
        self.generate_created_proxies()
        self.generate_altered_options()
        self.generate_altered_managers()
        self.generate_altered_db_table_comment()

        # Create the renamed fields and store them in self.renamed_fields.
        # They are used by create_altered_indexes(), generate_altered_fields(),
        # generate_removed_altered_index/unique_together(), and
        # generate_altered_index/unique_together().
        self.create_renamed_fields()
        # Create the altered indexes and store them in self.altered_indexes.
        # This avoids the same computation in generate_removed_indexes()
        # and generate_added_indexes().
        self.create_altered_indexes()
        self.create_altered_constraints()
        # Generate index removal operations before field is removed
        self.generate_removed_constraints()
        self.generate_removed_indexes()
        # Generate field renaming operations.
        self.generate_renamed_fields()
        self.generate_renamed_indexes()
        # Generate removal of foo together.
        self.generate_removed_altered_unique_together()
        self.generate_removed_altered_index_together()  # RemovedInDjango51Warning.
        # Generate field operations.
        self.generate_removed_fields()
        self.generate_added_fields()
        self.generate_altered_fields()
        self.generate_altered_order_with_respect_to()
        self.generate_altered_unique_together()
        self.generate_altered_index_together()  # RemovedInDjango51Warning.
        self.generate_added_indexes()
        self.generate_added_constraints()
        self.generate_altered_db_table()

        self._sort_migrations()
        self._build_migration_list(graph)
        self._optimize_migrations()

        return self.migrations

    def _prepare_field_lists(self):
        """
        Prepare field lists and a list of the fields that used through models
        in the old state so dependencies can be made from the through model
        deletion to the field that uses it.
        """
        self.kept_model_keys = self.old_model_keys & self.new_model_keys
        self.kept_proxy_keys = self.old_proxy_keys & self.new_proxy_keys
        self.kept_unmanaged_keys = self.old_unmanaged_keys & self.new_unmanaged_keys
        self.through_users = {}

Thought: Step 1 — what I'm investigating and why
- The bug report shows that a classmethod defined on a nested class (Profile.Capability.default) is serialized into migrations as appname.models.Capability.default (losing the outer class name). That makes the migration import an incorrect dotted path and fail at migrate time.
- The serialization of callables for migrations lives in django/db/migrations/serializer.py. I examined that file and the code paths used when building migration files (MigrationAutodetector -> deep_deconstruct -> serializer_factory -> FunctionTypeSerializer / TypeSerializer, etc.).

What I did (tool-driven walkthrough)
- I inspected django/db/migrations/autodetector.py to find where field defaults are deconstructed/serialized (deep_deconstruct is used).
- I inspected django/db/migrations/serializer.py to find the code that serializes callables and specifically bound class methods (FunctionTypeSerializer).
- I searched for other similar code spots that might need the same fix to make sure the fix is complete.

What I found (root cause)
- In django/db/migrations/serializer.py, FunctionTypeSerializer has a branch handling bound functions (class/staticmethods accessed from a class). The current code builds the dotted path for a class-bound function using klass.__name__:
  return "%s.%s.%s" % (module, klass.__name__, self.value.__name__), {"import %s" % module}
- For nested classes, klass.__name__ is only the innermost class name (e.g., 'Capability'). klass.__qualname__ contains the nested qualification (e.g., 'Profile.Capability'). Using __name__ therefore drops the outer class name and produces appname.models.Capability.default instead of the correct appname.models.Profile.Capability.default. This is exactly the behaviour seen in the bug report.
- TypeSerializer already uses __qualname__ correctly for types, and other serializers that need qualified names also use __qualname__ in various places. The only problematic location is the FunctionTypeSerializer branch that builds a path for a method bound to a class.

Complete fix — code change
- Change the FunctionTypeSerializer branch to use klass.__qualname__ instead of klass.__name__.

Patch (single-line change)
- File: django/db/migrations/serializer.py
- Change (in FunctionTypeSerializer.serialize):

From:
  return "%s.%s.%s" % (module, klass.__name__, self.value.__name__), {
      "import %s" % module
  }

To:
  return "%s.%s.%s" % (module, klass.__qualname__, self.value.__name__), {
      "import %s" % module
  }

Rationale:
- klass.__qualname__ preserves nesting ("Outer.Inner"), so the produced dotted name becomes e.g. "appname.models.Profile.Capability.default", and the import added ("import appname.models") matches how TypeSerializer imports module names and how Deconstructable serialization expects to reference values from imported modules.

Why this is a complete fix
- I searched the codebase for other instances where a class name was used to build a dotted path for a callable; the only occurrence doing this for bound functions was the line above. TypeSerializer already uses __qualname__, EnumSerializer uses __qualname__, and other related serializers handle names correctly.
- FunctionTypeSerializer also performs other checks (lambda, no module, local functions via "<" in qualname) which remain correct. This change only replaces klass.__name__ with klass.__qualname__ and doesn't alter other logic.

Additional notes / edge cases
- The returned string and import set from FunctionTypeSerializer are consumed as-is when writing the migration (the serializer returns (string, imports) directly). Using klass.__qualname__ (e.g., "Profile.Capability") appended to module (e.g., "appname.models") leads to the dotted path "appname.models.Profile.Capability.default" while the import remains "import appname.models" — consistent with other uses where a value in the module is referenced as module.<qualname>. The import is the module, not the full qualified class name, which is correct and consistent with TypeSerializer.
- This fix preserves behavior for non-nested classes (qualname == name).
- The change is safe for Python versions because __qualname__ exists on classes and functions.

Suggested test to add
- Add a unit test in tests for migrations serializer (e.g., tests/migrations/test_serializer.py) that asserts:
  - Given a nested class with a classmethod (or a @classmethod on a nested Enum/TextChoices), serializing that bound method uses the module + the class' qualname + function name. Example:

    class Profile(models.Model):
        class Capability(models.TextChoices):
            BASIC = ("BASIC", "Basic")

            @classmethod
            def default(cls):
                return [cls.BASIC]

    # Accessing the classmethod from the nested class:
    func = Profile.Capability.default
    string, imports = serializer_factory(func).serialize()
    assert "appname.models.Profile.Capability.default" in string
    assert "import appname.models" in imports

- Also add an integration-style test that runs makemigrations for a model where default is nested classmethod and ensures the generated migration contains the correct dotted path.

Summary (what to change)
- File to edit:
  - django/db/migrations/serializer.py
- Specific change:
  - In FunctionTypeSerializer.serialize(), replace klass.__name__ with klass.__qualname__ when building the dotted path for class-bound functions.

Why this resolves the bug
- Using __qualname__ includes outer class names, so nested class methods retain their nesting in the serialized dotted path and migrations will import/use the correct attribute path, e.g. appname.models.Profile.Capability.default.

If you want, I can produce a git-style diff/patch for serializer.py and example unit test code to add.

bug_report.Title: Nested class method used as Field.default serialized with incorrect dotted path in migrations
bug_report.Description: A classmethod defined on a nested class (e.g. Profile.Capability.default) when used as a Field.default is serialized into a migration with a flattened dotted path that omits the outer class (e.g. appname.models.Capability.default). This incorrect path is written into the generated migration and causes migration-time import errors.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect assumption: the serializer assumes a class' __name__ is sufficient to reference nested classes when building a dotted attribute path for a class-bound function. Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, FunctionTypeSerializer.serialize. Current produced pattern: "%s.%s.%s" % (module, klass.__name__, function_name). Correct relationship (what the serialized value should use): "%s.%s.%s" % (module, klass.__qualname__, function_name). Example consequence: instead of producing "appname.models.Profile.Capability.default" the serializer emits "appname.models.Capability.default", dropping the outer class name and producing an incorrect import target.

2) Consequence encoded in migration: the wrong dotted path (module + inner-class name + method) is written into migrations.AddField(... default=...), causing the migration to reference a non-existent top-level attribute and fail at migrate time. Location where the incorrect value appears: generated migration file (migrations/*.py) as the default argument for the field.
StepsToReproduce: Run python manage.py makemigrations to generate a migration
Inspect the generated migration file in migrations/ — observe the migrations.AddField entry for the field 'capabilities' and its default argument
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The generated migration should reference the nested class method with a fully qualified path including the outer class, e.g. "appname.models.Profile.Capability.default", so the attribute can be imported and resolved when the migration is applied.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The generated migration contains a flattened path that omits the outer class, e.g. "appname.models.Capability.default", and applying the migration fails because the referenced attribute does not exist at that path.
